name: Bebop
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize/deserialize latency of tiny/simple/complex POCOs (once and in bulk), comparing Bebop (Message and Struct variants) against Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json, Google.Protobuf, and MessagePack-CSharp, in an independent third-party benchmark repo.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize complex POCO once, mean latency: BebopStruct 166.1 ns vs Protobuf (Google.Protobuf, C#) 1,051.4 ns (~6.3x) and vs MessagePack-CSharp 1,584.6 ns (~9.5x). BebopMessage 231.7 ns is ~4.5x faster than Protobuf and ~6.8x faster than MessagePack (ratios derived from page data). The benchmark repo's README says Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization', and that on deserialization Protobuf 'becomes the slowest of the binary serializers'.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.13.1 DefaultJob (default Release build configuration, X64 RyuJIT), .NET SDK 6.0.100-preview.7.21379.14, runtime .NET 5.0.9 (5.0.921.35908). The net5.0 target sets no custom optimization properties in Benchmarks/Benchmarks.csproj. Packages: bebop 2.2.6, Google.Protobuf 3.17.3, MessagePack 2.3.75.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 1 CPU, 32 logical and 16 physical cores. BenchmarkDotNet reports the OS as Windows 10.0.22449.
tradeoffs: Bebop also targets TypeScript, Rust, Dart, C, and other languages via its own IDL/codegen, but the cited numeric evidence here is specifically for its C# implementation. Requires a `.bop` schema and code generation step (like Protobuf), unlike schema-less formats.
caveats: All numbers are C#: Bebop 2.2.6 vs the C# Protobuf (Google.Protobuf 3.17.3) and MessagePack-CSharp 2.3.75 runtimes on .NET 5.0.9, run in 2021. Bebop is now at v3.2.3 (2025-09-16) and .NET 5 is out of support, so current versions are untested. The benchmark repo is small (6 stars, last commit 2021-09-05) and publishes a single BenchmarkDotNet run on one desktop. The complex-POCO schemas are not like-for-like, which inflates Protobuf's complex-deserialize cost: Protobuf stores the child GUID as a string and uses google.protobuf.Timestamp sub-messages and double Percentage/Cost, Bebop uses native guid/date/float32, and MessagePack uses a decimal Cost. On the like-for-like tiny POCO (two int32 fields), Deserialize_Once_TinyPocos still shows BebopStruct 11.93 ns vs Protobuf 85.51 ns (~7.2x, derived). Serialization gains are much smaller, e.g. Serialize_Once_SimplePocos BebopMessage 94.40 ns vs Protobuf 100.82 ns (~1.07x) and Serialize_Once_ComplexPocos BebopStruct 239.2 ns vs Protobuf 926.5 ns (~3.9x) (derived). Bebop's serialize allocates more than both baselines: 1,032 B for complex serialize-once BebopStruct vs 400 B for Protobuf and 304 B for MessagePack. Bebop's own README claims ~10x over Protobuf in C# and TypeScript, but shows only a chart image.
found_via: WebSearch: query='Bebop serialization benchmark faster than protobuf flatbuffers github' -> github.com/ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks

verification.tier_reason: The independent ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks repo publishes its BenchmarkDotNet code against Google.Protobuf and MessagePack-CSharp: Benchmarks/Deserialize_Once_ComplexPocos.cs and 17 sibling classes, run by Benchmarks/Program.cs, with the schemas in SerializationEntities/. Each results page states the toolchain (.NET SDK 6.0.100-preview.7, .NET 5.0.9 X64 RyuJIT, BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.1 DefaultJob, which builds in Release) and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X), so it is A, the same call as the earlier Sep and simdunicode BenchmarkDotNet entries.
verification.notes: All six rows in the record match the page, and Bebop leads in all 18 BenchmarkResults tables. I pointed benchmark_url at the canonical /blob/main/ path (/blob/master/ 302-redirects to it) and set compared_against_cpp_std_directly to false, because the baselines are C# Protobuf/MessagePack runtimes, not the C++ standard library. The 6.3x complex figure is flattered by a schema mismatch (see caveats), but the like-for-like tiny-POCO table still shows ~7x, so the tier stays A.

Repo README states Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization' among the tested formats, and Protobuf becomes 'the slowest of the binary serializers' on deserialization.

name: bilrost
workload: Criterion micro-benchmark, 'log' dataset (HTTP request logs, many strings), serialize and deserialize a Rust struct via the rust_serialization_benchmark shootout.
claimed_speedup: log dataset: bilrost 0.1016.1 serialize 396.57 us (encode) / 300.26 us (prepend) vs prost 0.14.4 731.23 us (encode only) / 1.8883 ms (populate + encode): ~2.4x faster vs encode-only, ~6.3x vs populate+encode (derived from page data). Deserialize bilrost 2.1234 ms vs prost 2.6802 ms (decode) / 2.7061 ms (decode + convert): ~1.26x faster (derived from page data).

hardware: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 4 vCPUs, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
tradeoffs: Wire format is bilrost-specific, not protobuf-compatible; no zero-copy access mode; smaller ecosystem/tooling than protobuf.

name: bitcode
baseline: Protobuf (prost 0.14.4; Google's protobuf 4.36.1-release crate also on the page), FlatBuffers (flatbuffers 25.12.19), Cap'n Proto (capnp 0.27.0), MessagePack (rmp-serde 1.3.1); all are the Rust crates for those formats, not the C++ libraries
workload: Serialize/deserialize of the 'log' dataset (small HTTP-request-log-like structs with many strings) in djkoloski/rust_serialization_benchmark.
claimed_speedup: serialize 96.821 µs vs prost(protobuf) 731.23 µs (~7.6x), flatbuffers 763.63 µs (~7.9x), capnp 480.15 µs (~5.0x), rmp-serde(msgpack) 1.3179 ms (~13.6x); deserialize 1.1452 ms vs prost 2.6802 ms (~2.3x), rmp-serde 2.3829 ms (~2.1x); wire size 703,710 vs protobuf 884,628 bytes (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.100.0-nightly (a36d05efa 2026-09-09), LLVM 23.1.1; run as `cargo bench` by tools/bencher/src/main.rs with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native", and Cargo.toml [profile.bench] sets lto = true (otherwise release-profile defaults, opt-level 3); criterion with default settings
hardware: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 2 cores / 4 threads visible (Microsoft-hypervisor VM, GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runner per .github/workflows/bench.yml), x86_64
tradeoffs: Uses a custom derive macro and bit-packing (not byte-aligned), so it is not wire-compatible with protobuf/flatbuffers/msgpack/capnp and has a smaller ecosystem/no cross-language schema story.
caveats: Numbers come from one dataset ('log') of a four-dataset suite (README last updated 2026-09-10). On 'mesh', flatbuffers serializes faster than bitcode (371.26 us vs 1.2265 ms). capnp and flatbuffers are zero-copy formats with no owned deserialize on the page. Their access time is in ns, so only serialize is directly comparable for them. The prost figures are encode-only and decode-only; they leave out populate and convert, which favors prost. Unlike protobuf, flatbuffers and capnp, bitcode is Rust-only and not self-describing. Its README also makes a stable format across major versions a non-goal. The run is on a shared 2-core CI VM built with target-cpu=native. Cargo.toml and README say MIT OR Apache-2.0, but the repo holds only LICENSE-MIT; the README's LICENSE-APACHE link points to a file that does not exist.

name: flatcc
workload: flatbench schema/dataset (same schema and dataset as Google FPL's FlatBuffers benchmark), 1,000,000 iterations of encode and decode/traverse, optimized (-O3 -DNDEBUG) builds, comparing flatcc's generated C reader/builder against Google FlatBuffers' flatc-generated C++ code.
claimed_speedup: Encode: flatcc 626.074 ns/op vs flatc C++ 701.606 ns/op, about 1.12x faster (derived from page data). Decode/traverse: flatcc 28.652 ns/op vs flatc C++ 28.866 ns/op, effectively tied (~0.7%, derived from page data). The page itself says flatc and flatcc 'are close enough in performance for it not to matter much' and that flatcc's encode edge is 'likely due to less memory allocation'.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not named or versioned: the scripts use the system-default `c++` (CXX) with -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++11 for the flatc C++ build and `cc` (CC) with -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c11 for the flatcc C build (test/benchmark/benchflatc/run.sh, test/benchmark/benchflatcc/run.sh).
hardware: OS-X, 2.2 GHz Haswell Core i7 (JSON-benchmark section also reports numbers from the same hardware running Ubuntu in VirtualBox)
tradeoffs: flatcc generates C (not C++) code and produces a wire-compatible FlatBuffers binary, so it's usable from pure-C projects; the reported encode gain is attributed by the author mainly to reduced memory allocation rather than a fundamentally different algorithm. Only one schema/dataset is benchmarked, shared with Google's own FlatBuffers benchmark, not a broad corpus.
caveats: First-party benchmark (run and published by the flatcc maintainer); the compiler vendor/version is never stated, so it falls short of Tier A. The numbers are old: doc/benchmarks.md content dates from 2015-2016 (last content change 2016-02, moved to its own doc 2017-07) and has not been refreshed against current flatc/flatcc. test/benchmark/README.md says allocation strategies differ (the C++ builder is constructed on every iteration while the C builder is reset), which the page itself credits for flatcc's encode edge. The repo's raw Ubuntu run (test/benchmark/benchout-ubuntu.txt) reverses the encode result: flatcc 531.227 ns/op vs flatc C++ 515.662 ns/op (flatcc ~3% slower), while decode is flatcc 27.539 vs 29.967 ns/op (~8% faster). Overall the win over FlatBuffers C++ is marginal and platform-dependent.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/dvidelabs/flatcc/blob/master/doc/benchmarks.md (fetched via gh api repos/dvidelabs/flatcc/contents/doc/benchmarks.md)

verification.tier_reason: doc/benchmarks.md compares flatcc's C output with Google flatc-generated C++ on the flatbench schema, and the benchmark code is public (test/benchmark/benchflatc/run.sh, test/benchmark/benchflatcc/run.sh, driven by scripts/benchmark.sh). Flags (-O3 -DNDEBUG) and CPU (2.2 GHz Haswell Core i7) are stated, but the compiler is never named or versioned (scripts just call the system `cc`/`c++`), so this is first-party with partial methodology: C, not A.
verification.notes: Numbers on the page match the record exactly; the ratios are correctly marked as derived. Downgraded A to C only because the compiler is unnamed (the record's own caveats admitted this); metadata (Apache-2.0, 769 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, not a fork, not archived) all check out.

name: hpp-proto
workload: Google Benchmark (benchmarks/benchmark.cpp) runs deserialize, set_message, serialize-only and set_message+serialize. It uses GoogleMessage1 (proto2 and proto3) from the protobuf v3.6.0 benchmarks.proto schema, with a single ~220-byte message filled in code by set_message_google, not the v3.6.0 dataset files. There is also a 'big' variant with 512- and 2048-byte strings, and a 1000-element packed repeated uint64 message with random values. Google protobuf runs in regular and arena modes; hpp-proto runs in regular and non-owning modes.
claimed_speedup: Linux numbers from the README prose (i9-11950H, gcc 13.3.0, protobuf 33.2). Deserialize, google arena vs hpp-proto non-owning: proto2 210 ns vs 141 ns (~1.5x), proto3 252 ns vs 160 ns (~1.6x). Deserialize regular: proto2 215 vs 210 ns, proto3 251 vs 212 ns. repeated_packed: google regular 4164 ns vs hpp-proto regular 2624 ns (~1.6x); google arena 4263 ns vs hpp-proto non-owning 2550 ns. Set_message+serialize, google arena vs hpp-proto non-owning: proto2 186 vs 99.6 ns (~1.9x), proto3 223 vs 121 ns (~1.8x); regular: proto2 185 vs 139 ns, proto3 219 vs 148 ns. Google is faster on serialize-only: proto2 64.5 vs 85.1 ns, proto3 98.8 vs 102 ns. (Ratios derived from page data.)
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17.0.0 (Mac); gcc 13.3.0 (Linux); Google protobuf 33.2. Optimization flags and build type are not stated for the published results. The ReadMe run command sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE; CMakePresets.json has a 'benchmark' preset with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, but it is not tied to the published numbers.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (Mac); 11th Gen Intel Core i9-11950H @ 2.60GHz (Linux)
tradeoffs: Requires C++23 compiler (Clang 19+ / GCC 13+); Google protobuf still wins on pure serialize-only of already-constructed objects; biggest gains require the non-owning/arena mode, which changes ownership semantics vs stock generated protobuf classes
caveats: First-party benchmark. Flags and build type are not stated for the published numbers. The README prose numbers do not exactly match the committed benchmarks/Linux_bench.result. For example, in the raw file repeated_packed takes 3966 ns wall / 3852 ns CPU for google regular (the prose says 4164) and 2650 / 2511 ns for hpp-proto regular (the prose says 2624). The workload is one small in-code GoogleMessage1 plus synthetic packed data, not the v3.6.0 dataset files. Google wins serialize-only (proto2 64.5 vs 85.1 ns). The headline gains compare hpp-proto non-owning mode with Google arena mode; in regular deserialize mode the gap is small (proto2 215 vs 210 ns). The Mac (M1 Pro) results have the same shape. Only two machines were tested, with no variance reported.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'HFT low latency binary serialization C++ library github faster than protobuf' surfaced huangminghuang/hpp-proto; opened repo and benchmarks/ReadMe.md via gh api

verification.tier_reason: benchmarks/ReadMe.md compares hpp-proto directly with Google protobuf 33.2 using public code (benchmarks/benchmark.cpp, Google Benchmark, built by benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt) and states the compilers (Apple clang 17.0.0, gcc 13.3.0) and CPUs (M1 Pro, i9-11950H). No optimization flags or build type are stated for the published numbers: the page's own run command (`cmake -B build -DHPP_PROTO_BENCHMARKS=ON`) sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, and only an unlinked 'benchmark' preset in CMakePresets.json sets Release. That rules out A, and first-party numbers are C.
verification.notes: The numbers match benchmarks/ReadMe.md (Linux section). The main branch's last commit is 2026-08-03; the 2026-09-25 date comes from a non-default cflite-corpus branch. If the orchestrator accepts the CMakePresets.json 'benchmark' preset (Release) as the stated flags, the entry would meet A, but the page itself states no flags.

name: minicbor
workload: Criterion micro-benchmark, 'log' dataset (HTTP request logs, many strings), serialize and deserialize a Rust struct via the rust_serialization_benchmark shootout.
claimed_speedup: log dataset: minicbor 2.3.0 serialize 405.77 us vs rmp-serde 1.3.1 1.3179 ms (~3.2x faster, derived from page data); deserialize 2.3448 ms vs 2.3829 ms (on par). Vs prost 0.14.4: ~1.8x vs encode-only 731.23 us, ~4.7x vs populate+encode 1.8883 ms (derived). Vs the common serde CBOR crate ciborium 0.2.2: serialize 3.3751 ms (~8.3x) and deserialize 10.862 ms (~4.6x) (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.100.0-nightly (a36d05efa 2026-09-09), LLVM 23.1.1; Criterion via cargo bench, [profile.bench] lto = true
hardware: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 4 vCPUs, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
tradeoffs: CBOR-based (self-describing, larger than a tight custom binary format); designed for no_std/embedded use; deserialize speed is not clearly ahead of msgpack, only serialize is.
caveats: Serialize-only win over MessagePack's rmp-serde: deserialize is on par on log and slightly slower on mesh (9.4268 vs 9.2506 ms) and minecraft_savedata (2.6924 vs 2.3727 ms). Other MessagePack crates in the same table (msgpacker 266.04 us, zerompk 269.23 us serialize; 2.0663 / 1.8129 ms deserialize) beat minicbor, so it is faster than the incumbent rmp-serde, not than MessagePack in general. Its clearest win is over ciborium (CBOR). Output is smaller than ciborium's (817830 vs 1407835 bytes on log), so the encodings differ. Licensed Blue Oak Model License 1.0.0, OSI-approved on 2024-01-19; GitHub reports NOASSERTION.
found_via: Blogs/talks discovery of https://david.kolo.ski/blog/rkyv-is-faster-than/ led to the rust_serialization_benchmark shootout, where minicbor is harvested as a top performer against messagepack/protobuf on the log dataset.

name: msgspec-serde
workload: Official-API comparison: a FlatBuffers 'Monster'-style schema at three profiles (small 100, medium 5,408 and large 1,118,720 logical elements), measuring encode of a materialized model, decode to a materialized model, lazy-view selected-field reads and lazy-view full traversal, with pyperf (6 processes x 5 values) on one isolated core. The separate 1,000-object File/Directory graph benchmark (16- and 256-value NumPy vectors) compares msgspec/orjson/ormsgpack and msgspec-serde's own JSON, MessagePack and FlatBuffers codecs, not the official FlatBuffers API.
claimed_speedup: benchmarks.md text: 'approximately 20–22 times faster to encode and 11–13 times faster to materialize', selected-field access 'about 1.2 times faster', full traversal '1.5 to 2.9 times faster' than the official Python FlatBuffers API. The chart on the same page (benchmarks/images/python-flatbuffers-comparison.png, small/medium/large profiles) shows slightly lower figures: encode 18.7x/21.8x/20.7x, decode-to-model 10.6x/11.8x/11.6x, selected fields 1.2x/1.2x/1.3x, full traversal 1.4x/2.5x/2.8x.
compiler_and_flags: CPython 3.13.5; msgspec 0.21.1, NumPy 2.5.2, Python FlatBuffers 25.12.19, flatc 23.5.2, msgspec-serde 0.1.0. The speed-critical path is a Rust pyo3 extension built by maturin with profile=release (pyproject.toml, rust/Cargo.toml, edition 2024); the rustc version is not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8650U CPU, single isolated core, Linux
stars_or_usage: 1 star (repo created 2026-08-25; v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 released 2026-08-30)
tradeoffs: Python-only; the speedup is specific to msgspec-serde's generated Struct/View codec path vs the stock Python flatbuffers package's Object API, not a change to the FlatBuffers wire format itself; at 256-value vectors the plain FlatBuffers decode path is fastest overall, not msgspec-serde; requires flatc for IDL codegen

name: qdf (Quick Data Format)
baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, MessagePack (wire size); MessagePack and Go encoding/json (encode/decode speed)
workload: Wire size and allocations for batches of realistic structured records (OTLP traces, logs, RTB bids, events, IoT float series) encoded record-for-record by json/msgpack/protobuf/flatbuffers/qdf on the same fixtures, via a reproducible `scripts/compare.sh` benchmark suite.
claimed_speedup: Wire size at the qdf_compression tier vs protobuf on 5 batch fixtures: RTB 203,360 vs 327,700 B (-38%), IoT 148,177 vs 207,562 B (-29%), OTLP 179,181 vs 561,860 B (-68%), Logs 62,149 vs 156,479 B (-60%), Events 39,639 vs 64,978 B (-39%), i.e. up to 68% smaller than Protobuf. On a 5,000-user Active-Directory export, qdf OptBalanced gives 1,830 KB, 6.6 ms encode and 7.9 ms decode, against encoding/json at 3,833 KB / 14.1 ms / 57.8 ms and msgpack at 3,370 KB / 8.7 ms / 16.7 ms. The page's summary: 2.1x smaller and 2.1x faster encode than json, ~7x faster decode than json, and 1.8x smaller with ~2x faster decode than msgpack. qdf is not faster than protobuf or FlatBuffers. Per the page, protobuf and FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput and FlatBuffers wins encode allocation outright. Protobuf wins single-tiny-message size and max encode throughput. qdf_balanced and qdf_compression do not win on allocation, though qdf_speed allocates less than protobuf on 4 of 5 fixtures.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 gc toolchain (docs/BENCH.md: Go 1.26.0), default build. scripts/compare.sh runs `go test -run='^$' -bench='RTB|IoT|OTLP|Logs|Events' -benchmem -count=6` in bench/ plus `EMIT_MEM=1 go test -run=TestMemoryReport`. go.mod and bench/go.mod now require go 1.27.0, so the published 2026-06-01 numbers predate the current modules.
hardware: Intel Core i7-9750H @ 2.6 GHz, darwin/amd64 (laptop)
tradeoffs: Go-only, pure-Go, no schema/IDL (struct-tag based, alpha format that 'still moves'). Wins are on batches with cross-record repetition; single tiny messages favor Protobuf/FlatBuffers per author's own comparison. Compression tier trades encode CPU for size (e.g. ~70 MB/s vs ~1100 MB/s for the balanced tier on float data).

Against Protobuf the win is wire size, not speed: the page concedes that protobuf and FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput. It is not the fastest Rust crate overall. name: YaFF (Yet another Flat Format)
workload: Median time to read every field out of an already-serialized buffer, for flat messages (10/100 uint64 fields) and a 3-level hierarchical message under hot (~2KB working set) and cold (~512MB working set) access patterns, using google/benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Flat Layout reads are ~25-50x faster than Protobuf and ~2-2.5x faster than FlatBuffers on flat messages (e.g. 100-field flat read: 25.99ns YaFF vs 1383.74ns Protobuf vs 54.81ns FlatBuffers); hierarchical hot access is ~25x faster than Protobuf and ~3.5x faster than FlatBuffers
compiler_and_flags: Clang 20.1.8, CMake Release build (CMake's Release default is -O3 -DNDEBUG; no -march or other extra flags in the benchmark CMakeLists), C++20; google/benchmark 1.9.5, FlatBuffers 24.12.23, Protobuf >=5.26 via Conan (the exact Protobuf version is not stated)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7713, x86-64
tradeoffs: Still requires an existing .proto schema (built as a companion physical layout for Protobuf, not a schema replacement); adds adaptive-layout complexity; C++ only today, multi-language bindings are roadmap items
caveats: Very young project (repo created 2026-04-07), first-party benchmark on a single machine (EPYC 7713, DDR4); the authors say only the ratios generalize. The Protobuf timings include ParseFromString/ParseFromArray of the whole message on every iteration, because Protobuf cannot read fields without parsing. So this compares zero-copy field access with parse-plus-access, not serialization speed. The win shrinks sharply with cold random access (~512 MB working set): 206.64 vs 387.48 ns vs Protobuf (~1.9x) and vs 300.13 ns for FlatBuffers (~1.45x). With hot hierarchical access and hand-cached access chains, FlatBuffers is only ~2.1x slower (20.89 vs 9.81 ns), not 3.5x (derived from page data). The Protobuf version is not pinned (Conan protobuf/[>=5.26]). GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the standard Apache-2.0 notice (Copyright 2026 YANDEX LLC).

name: Cornflakes
baseline: Protobuf, FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto via the pure-Rust crates protobuf 3.0.3 (rust-protobuf), flatbuffers 2.1.2 and capnp 0.13.6 (cf-kv/Cargo.toml); Redis handwritten serialization for Table 3
workload: Custom Rust key-value store and echo server serving a CDN image-object trace (1M objects, 1KB-116MB, mean ~20KB), a Twitter cache trace, and Redis GET/MGET/LRANGE commands, over kernel-bypass 100Gb NICs
claimed_speedup: CDN image trace (Table 2), in thousands of objects/s: Cornflakes 366.5 vs Cap'n Proto 161.0, FlatBuffers 181.2 and Protobuf 186.1; the paper says 97-128% higher. Twitter cache trace (Fig. 7): 15.4-45.9% higher throughput than the three baselines, at a p99 of 52 us for Cornflakes vs 53 us (FlatBuffers, Protobuf) and 61 us (Cap'n Proto). Google bytes-size trace (Table 1), in thousands of req/s: no win for small values. Cornflakes has 844.7 vs Protobuf 852.5 (1 value) and 727.2 vs 741.9 (1-4 values). It leads only at 1-8 values (584.5 vs 583.8) and 1-16 values (441.2 vs 412.0). Redis (Table 3) is measured against Redis's own handwritten serialization, not Protobuf, FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto: 15-40.1% higher throughput (get 23.37 vs 18.49 Gbps, mget-2 14.12 vs 12.27, lrange-2 15.07 vs 10.75).
compiler_and_flags: rustc version not pinned: install/install-rust.sh installs 1.70.0 and then runs `rustup default stable`. Cargo.toml [profile.release] sets opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1, panic="abort"; the Makefile builds with --release unless DEBUG=y. The paper states no compiler.
hardware: 2x 24-core AMD EPYC 7402P 2.80GHz servers (CloudLab c6525-100g), Dual-port Mellanox ConnectX-5Ex 100Gb NICs, jumbo frames MTU 9000, Ubuntu 20.04 / Linux 5.04
tradeoffs: Rust-primary implementation; README states C-bindings to the serialization code exist but this was not independently verified for C++ usability; requires DPDK or Mellanox/Intel ICE NIC drivers and hugepages (kernel-bypass networking), so it is not a drop-in library without specialized datacenter NIC hardware; zero-copy only helps once field/object sizes exceed the measured ~512-byte threshold — for small objects Cornflakes only ties the baselines, it does not beat them
caveats: The baselines are pure-Rust implementations (rust-protobuf 3.0.3, the flatbuffers 2.1.2 Rust runtime, capnproto-rust 0.13.6), not wrappers around the canonical C++ libraries. The C++ installs in install/install-libraries.sh are used only for the protoc/flatc/capnp code generators. All systems run over Cornflakes's own kernel-bypass UDP stack, with a per-library network API. There is no gain on small-object workloads (Table 1: within 98% of Protobuf at 1 and 1-4 values). The Redis gains are against Redis's handwritten serialization. The rustc version is not pinned. The repo has no LICENSE file. The default branch's last commit is 2023-07-27; a non-default 'timetrace' branch has a commit from 2024-01-19.

The Cargo.toml release profile gives the flags, but the rustc version is not pinned: install/install-rust.sh installs 1.70.0 and then runs `rustup default stable`. name: greenpack
baseline: Protocol Buffers (Go implementations: gogo/protobuf gogofaster, golang/protobuf, DeDiS/protobuf); FlatBuffers Go and Cap'n Proto Go are also in the table
workload: Marshal/Unmarshal microbenchmarks of a fixed struct (name, birthday, phone, siblings, spouse, money) across ~20 Go serialization libraries, using Go's testing/benchmark tool, in the companion go_serialization_benchmarks shootout repo.
claimed_speedup: This claim holds for writes only. GreenPackMarshal takes 129 ns/op with 0 B/op, against 152 ns/op with 64 B/op for GogoprotobufMarshal (~15% faster, derived from page data). It is also faster than golang/protobuf (GoprotobufMarshal, 500 ns/op), DeDiS/protobuf (ProtobufMarshal, reflection-based, 936 ns/op), FlatBuffers Go (379 ns/op) and Cap'n Proto via glycerine/go-capnproto (498 ns/op). ZebraPack, by the same author, is faster at 120 ns/op. The README's '6% faster reads' does not measure greenpack. It rests on GreenPackUnmarshal (224 ns/op) against GogoprotobufUnmarshal (240 ns/op), but BenchmarkGreenPackUnmarshal calls ZebraPack's ZMarshalMsg/ZUnmarshalMsg, not GreenUnmarshalMsg. That row is therefore a second run of BenchmarkZebraPackUnmarshal, which measured 236 ns/op in the same run.
compiler_and_flags: The README header says 'Go 1.8beta2'. The August 2017 commit that added greenpack (de65278) replaced the result tables but left that header from the January 2017 run unchanged, so the Go version of the greenpack run is unconfirmed. The command is go test -bench='.*' ./ and no other flags are given.
hardware: 3.1 GHz Intel Core i7 (MacBook Pro 13"); no CPU model number stated
tradeoffs: Pure Go, code-generation based (like msgp/msgpack), msgpack2-compatible wire format for cross-language interoperability. Modest win margin (6-15%) over Protobuf, not a dramatic speedup; author explicitly notes ZebraPack and CapNProto/Gencode can be faster in some cases.
caveats: These are first-party numbers: greenpack's author ran them in his own fork (glycerine/go_serialization_benchmarks, 8 stars, last commit 2017-08-05). The upstream alecthomas suite does not include greenpack. The read comparison is invalid because of a copy-paste bug: BenchmarkGreenPackUnmarshal uses ZebraPack's generated ZMarshalMsg/ZUnmarshalMsg. The throughput columns confirm this: the 'greenpack' unmarshal payload is ~59 bytes, the same as ZebraPack's, while greenpack marshal emits ~142 bytes. Only the write result measures greenpack. The margins are small next to run-to-run noise: the earlier run had ZebraPackUnmarshal at 227 ns/op and Gogoprotobuf at 232 ns/op. Hardware and Go version (2017, Go 1.8-era) are dated. The only baselines are Go protobuf implementations, not C++ protobuf. greenpack itself is still maintained, with a last commit on 2026-01-23.

name: JSON BinPack
baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, MessagePack (and Apache Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers)
workload: Encoded size of 27 real-world JSON documents from SchemaStore, measured uncompressed and after GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 and LZMA -9. There is one document per JSON Taxonomy class (tier x type x redundancy x structure), and each is encoded with JSON BinPack (schema-driven and schema-less) and 13 other formats. JSON BinPack was run through the TypeScript proof of concept (npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x), not the C++ code in this repo.
claimed_speedup: This is a size result only; nothing is claimed about speed. In all 27 documents, JSON BinPack (schema-driven) produced the smallest or tied-smallest uncompressed encoding. The comparison covered Protocol Buffers (Python protobuf 3.12.4), FlatBuffers (flatc 1.12.0), Cap'n Proto 0.7.0 (binary and packed), MessagePack (Python msgpack 1.0.0), Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers and JSON. On four documents it ties with Avro and/or Protocol Buffers. Example: the ESLint configuration encodes to 64 bytes against 1,141 bytes of JSON (~94.4% smaller, derived from page data). Across the 27 documents the median reduction against JSON is ~86.8% and the mean ~78.8% (derived from page data; arXiv 2211.12799 reports 86.7% and 78.7%). The schema-driven uncompressed output is smaller than JSON compressed with GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 or LZMA -9 in all 27 documents (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Dual-licensed (AGPL-3.0-or-later or paid commercial license) — AGPL's network-copyleft is a real adoption barrier for closed-source SaaS use. Space-efficiency focused, not runtime-efficiency focused; project's own FAQ recommends FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto instead when zero-copy runtime speed matters. Requires JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions for schema-driven mode.
caveats: The win is size, not speed. The README concedes runtime efficiency and recommends FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto for extreme runtime efficiency or zero-copy use. The benchmark covers 27 documents; the '400+ SchemaStore documents' figure comes from arXiv 2201.03051, which does not include JSON BinPack. The benchmark ran the archived TypeScript proof of concept (jviotti/jsonbinpack-poc, npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x, February 2022; the page lists 1.1.1 and the Dockerfile installs 1.1.2). The current C++ implementation in this repo is not measured, and the wire format may have changed since. The benchmark is first-party, by the project's author, and the arXiv write-ups are preprints, not peer-reviewed. The README says the MSc dissertation won the 2022 CAR Hoare Prizes. The competitors are older versions (protobuf 3.12.4, flatc 1.12.0, Cap'n Proto 0.7.0). No compiler or hardware is stated, which is irrelevant for byte counts. The license is dual: AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial.
found_via: arXiv: search_query=abs:%22FlatBuffers%22+OR+abs:%22Cap%27n+Proto%22 -> arXiv:2211.12799 'Benchmarking JSON BinPack' -> github.com/sourcemeta/jsonbinpack

verification.tier_reason: This is the project author's own benchmark (sourcemeta/json-size-benchmark, whose Dockerfile pins the implementation versions). The arXiv write-ups 2211.12799 and 2201.03051 are preprints with no journal reference, so they are not peer-reviewed; an MSc dissertation is not a peer-reviewed paper either. No compiler, flags or CPU are given, which matters little for a size benchmark, but those are the tier rules. That makes it first-party with partial methodology: C.
verification.notes: This is a scope rejection (not-faster): every number checks out, but JSON BinPack's claim is encoded size, and its own README hands runtime speed to FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto. Under the keep-flagged-entries policy, it could stay with this shortcoming, tier C. Another shortcoming: the benchmark measured the archived TypeScript proof of concept, not this C++ repo. name: Karmem
workload: Go testing benchmarks in benchmark/ (main_test.go, main_fbs.go, main_km.go). They encode and decode, through the object API, a Monsters root of 1000 monsters; each monster has a 100-element Vec3 path, a 100-byte inventory, weapons, hitbox and status arrays. DecodeSumVec3 sums the path vectors with zero-copy readers. The FlatBuffers side uses the Go object API (Pack / UnPackTo) with a 'similar', not identical, schema. Runs cover native Go and a TinyGo-compiled WASI module inside wazero, on an Apple M1.
claimed_speedup: README headline: 'almost 10 times faster than Google Flatbuffers'. benchstat, FlatBuffers (old) vs Karmem (new), Apple M1. Native: EncodeObjectAPI 2.54ms -> 0.51ms (-79.85%, ~5x), DecodeObjectAPI 3.57ms -> 0.20ms (-94.30%, ~18x), DecodeSumVec3 1.44ms -> 0.16ms (-88.86%, ~9x). WASM on wazero: EncodeObjectAPI 17.2ms -> 4.0ms (-76.51%, ~4.3x), DecodeObjectAPI 50.7ms -> 1.9ms (-96.18%, ~27x), DecodeSumVec3 5.74ms -> 0.75ms (-86.87%, ~7.7x). The x-ratios are derived from page data. Allocations are zero only natively: 0 vs 1.00k allocs/op for encode and 0 vs 110k for decode. Under WASM allocs/op are about equal (4 vs 4 encode, 4 vs 5 decode).
compiler_and_flags: Go and TinyGo versions for the README run are unstated. benchmark/go.mod declares go 1.18 and FlatBuffers Go v2.0.6; CI (.builds/ubuntu.yml) uses go1.18.4 on linux/amd64, but that is not the M1 run. Native: go test -tags fbs|km -bench=. -benchmem -benchtime=5s -count 5. WASM: tinygo build -target wasi -gc conservative --no-debug -opt 2 -scheduler none, run under wazero. Results compared with benchstat.

tradeoffs: Designed primarily for WebAssembly host/guest data sharing (TinyGo/WASM), not general-purpose RPC; author states FlatBuffers 'causes panics due to lack of bound-checking' motivating the project. No Rust/C++ note beyond Go/TinyGo/AssemblyScript targets claimed in docs.

The schemas are 'similar', not identical: Karmem uses inline fixed arrays ([5]float64, [4]Weapon) where FlatBuffers uses vectors. Hacker News commenters (item 32302120) questioned the methodology and the '10x' claim, and the author did not answer those points in the thread. The README warns that the API is not stable. No commits since 2023-03-03 (>3 years), so abandoned.

name: Microsoft Bond (Compact Binary v1)

claimed_speedup: JSON Resume: Bond Compact Binary v1 is 2256 bytes vs FlatBuffers 3116 (~28% smaller), Cap'n Proto binary 3152 (~28% smaller) and Cap'n Proto packed 2549 (~11% smaller). Protobuf is smaller than Bond at 2225 bytes. CircleCI-blank: Bond 10 bytes vs FlatBuffers 20 and Cap'n Proto binary 24; packed Cap'n Proto is 6 and Protobuf 5. Across all 27 documents, Bond is smaller than FlatBuffers on 27/27, than binary Cap'n Proto on 26/27 and than packed Cap'n Proto on 21/27, but smaller than Protobuf on only 1/27 (geojson). name: s2s (ziglibs)
baseline: Protocol Buffers (Arwalk/zig-protobuf 5.0.0, generated from the suite's shared benchmark_v2.proto); MessagePack (serde.zig 1.2.1 backend) also compared
workload: Serialize+deserialize time on 5 shared fixtures (document, event, message, strings, telemetry) from the suite's common IDLs. Single-instance and 100-instance cells, bytes and stream modes, 100 reps per cell with 1 warmup, in the GLD.SerializerBenchmark Zig runner
claimed_speedup: Serialize+deserialize time in run 2026-09-14-134825, 100-instance cells: 1.13-1.99x faster than zig-protobuf on all 5 fixtures in stream mode over all trials (document 1.88x, event 1.43x, message 1.43x, strings 1.13x, telemetry 1.99x). With bytes mode and the dashboard's default IQR filter it is 1.12-2.02x, and single-instance cells give 1.21-2.09x. Against serde.zig's MessagePack backend: 1.4-2.2x faster on 4 of 5 fixtures, slower on strings (0.92x). (all derived from page data) The Cap'n Proto '12.9-17.9x' figure is dropped: that row calls the C++ runtime through a C bridge compiled with no -O flag.

hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12800H (20 logical cores, powersave governor), 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04, Linux 6.8.0-138

This was a single-session run (the suite's own claim level L1) on a laptop CPU under the powersave governor. Protobuf's timed decode also converts the generated message back into the suite struct, while s2s decodes straight into it. s2s payloads are about 1.1-1.7x larger than protobuf's, and s2s serialize is slower than protobuf's on 'strings'. s2s loses to zig-flatbuffers on strings and telemetry, to msgpack.zig on strings (about a tie elsewhere), and to the suite's in-tree comptime-bin encoder on every fixture. The Cap'n Proto row is not a fair baseline because of the unoptimized C bridge and extra copies. s2s is a Zig-only format; its README calls it complete only for the 'trivial' case.

name: Simple Binary Encoding (SBE)
workload: Serialize/deserialize a small trading domain object (one Account with Wallet and 3 Orders, 128 bytes in memory) in chronoxor's CppBenchmark-based CppSerialization suite. SBE encodes it to 138 bytes and Protobuf to 120 bytes. Both timings include converting from/to the plain C++ domain model: Protobuf builds a fresh message per operation without an arena, while SBE encodes in place into a fixed 1 KB buffer. Also compared: Cap'n Proto, FastBinaryEncoding, FlatBuffers, zpp::bits and JSON (RapidJSON).
claimed_speedup: ~9.2x faster serialize (35 ns vs 322 ns) and ~6.75x faster deserialize (52 ns vs 351 ns) than Protobuf (ratios derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: chronoxor/CppSerialization suite at commit 8f6e4240 with sbe-all-1.35.6.jar; CMake sets C++23; compiler and optimization flags not stated. SBE_NO_BOUNDS_CHECK is never defined, so SBE bounds checks were likely on.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (10 cores, reported 2.4 GHz), 32 GiB RAM, macOS (Darwin 24.5.0). All 15 CppBenchmark reports in the README come from this one machine, run on 2025-07-16
tradeoffs: Requires an SBE XML schema and code generator; designed around FIX-derived low-latency financial messaging, less flexible than Protobuf for evolving/optional fields
caveats: The numbers come from a small third-party shootout (chronoxor/CppSerialization, 167 stars) run by the author of a competing format (FastBinaryEncoding), not by SBE's team. SBE's own sbe-benchmarks (Car/MarketData, C++ and Java) do not compare against Protobuf. Compiler and flags are not stated, and everything ran on a single Apple M1 Pro on 2025-07-16 with SBE 1.40.1. The message is tiny (138 bytes), so the results may not generalize to larger or variable-length-heavy messages. zpp::bits was marginally faster in the same table (34/37 ns).

name: Imprint
baseline: Protobuf (Rust prost 0.12 implementation, per the since-removed benches/Cargo.toml)
workload: Criterion micro-benchmarks on fake Product/Order records at sizes 1, 5 and 10. Merge: decode two records and write an enriched combined record (protobuf: prost decode of both, clone into an EnrichedOrder, re-encode; Imprint: read both, directory merge, write). Projection: read one record and write a field subset (protobuf: decode and re-encode a SimpleProduct; Imprint: project 6 fields and write).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Imprint performs up to 76% better than protobuf at merging two records', with Imprint merge time roughly constant while protobuf grows with record size. Merge chart (approximate read-off): protobuf ~1000 / ~2140 / ~3450 vs Imprint ~785 / ~800 / ~800 at merge_size_1/5/10, so ~4.3x at the largest size (derived from page data, approximate). The projection chart has no ratio in the text. It shows Imprint SLOWER at project_size_1 (~580 vs protobuf ~360) and faster only at size 5 (~650 vs ~890) and size 10 (~625 vs ~1530) (approximate read-off). The chart's y-axis unit is labeled ambiguously as 'ns/µs'.
tradeoffs: Field directory adds roughly 3-5 bytes/field of overhead versus protobuf's ~1-varint tag/field, so wire size is slightly larger; schema-less reads require scanning a directory; optimized for compose/project (stream-join) access patterns rather than raw sequential encode/decode throughput
caveats: The README shows only chart images plus one headline percentage. Compiler/toolchain, flags and CPU model are not stated. The baseline is Rust prost 0.12, not Google's C++ protobuf. The protobuf comparison harness (benches/src/serialization.rs, benches/Cargo.toml with prost 0.12) was removed from the repo in PR #31 (2025-05-28): the current benches/serde_bench.rs benchmarks Imprint alone, so the charted comparison is reproducible only from git history (commit f42484cf). The protobuf merge path also clones both decoded messages, which adds allocation to the baseline. Imprint is slower than protobuf for projection at the smallest record size. The public benchmark harness (benchmarks/benchmark1.ts) only compares JSON vs JSBT; the Protobuf, MsgPack and CBOR rows in the README tables have no published harness. The repeated dataset is built to favor deduplication (id i%100, name i%50, one shared scores array, identical tags/meta), and sizes are uncompressed (no gzip/zstd comparison). name: Lite³ (lite3)
workload: Three external suites, forked and run by the Lite³ author and linked from the README. (1) Cista++ cpp-serialization-benchmark: serialize, deserialize and traverse a node/edge graph, vs FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, cereal, zpp::bits and Cista++. (2) simdjson bench_ondemand queries on twitter.json (~632 kB): top_tweet, partial_tweets, find_tweet and distinct_user_id, vs simdjson, yyjson and RapidJSON, with Lite³ on pre-converted binary data. (3) kostya/benchmarks JSON coordinate sum (~115 MB). The lite3 repo has no harness of its own.
claimed_speedup: Cista++ cpp-serialization-benchmark fork, graph with 1870 nodes: serialize+deserialize takes 7.79 ms for the Lite³ Buffer API vs 1887.49 ms for FlatBuffers (242x, derived from page data; this is the project's '242x'). Serialize is 3.02 vs 1845.8 ms (611x, derived), deserialize/verify 4.77 vs 41.69 ms (8.7x, derived) and traverse 79.39 vs 90.53 ms (1.14x, derived). Message size is 38.069 MB vs 62.998 MB. zpp::bits (4.66 ms) and Cista++ offset slim (3.96 ms) beat Lite³ on serialize+deserialize. The 'up to 120x' claim is simdjson On-Demand find_tweet at 53937 ns vs 448 ns for the Lite³ Buffer API (120x, derived) on twitter.json. In that test Lite³ queries data pre-converted to its binary format while the other libraries parse JSON.
compiler_and_flags: Cista++ fork: g++-11 with CMake Release for the benchmark; liblite3 is built by its Makefile default (-O2 -DNDEBUG). The simdjson and kostya forks state no compiler or flags.
tradeoffs: Core library is C, not C++ (a separate C++ port, jasoncoposky/lite3-cpp, exists but has only 1 star and is unverified for the same performance); schemaless self-describing design costs ~40% extra size vs raw JSON on the cited Twitter dataset; O(log n) rather than O(1) field access

name: MTS-1 (Lightweight Delta-Encoded Telemetry Format)
workload: Synthetic telemetry payload size comparison (storage footprint) of MTS-1 against JSON, JSON Lines, CBOR, MessagePack, and Protocol Buffers for low-resource/offline-first system health monitoring.
claimed_speedup: Reported ~5.4% smaller than MessagePack and 74.6-74.7% smaller than JSON on the paper's synthetic S1 dataset (MTS-1 1.39 MB vs MessagePack 1.47 MB). Protocol Buffers was explicitly excluded from quantitative testing by the authors ('schema compilation requirements incompatible with dynamic monitoring scenarios').
tradeoffs: No throughput/latency numbers at all, only payload size; Protobuf, one of the category's core baselines, was deliberately not benchmarked. No implementation language, code repository, or reference implementation could be found.
caveats: No code repository or specification is published. The only reproducibility aid is the author's email. This is a January 2026 single-author arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed) with synthetic datasets only (10k/20k/50k payloads generated from Magenta metric samples). The win over MessagePack is modest: 1,390,000 vs 1,469,521 bytes on S1 (5.4%). The MTS-1 sizes are exactly 139 B per payload on every dataset (1,390,000 / 2,780,000 / 6,950,000 bytes), which suggests computed rather than measured values. MTS-1+LZ4 is larger than plain MTS-1. MTS-1 drops changes below a threshold epsilon, so it is lossy by design, although the paper claims identical semantic information. The abstract says encoding cost was compared, but no encoding-time results are reported. Protocol Buffers was excluded from the quantitative tests.

name: cpp-yyjson
workload: Read (parse a document and visit every element) and write (serialize a parsed document back to text) across ten JSON documents (0.1-66.4 MB, number-heavy to string-heavy) from the yyjson_benchmark dataset, measured with Google Benchmark (median of 11-101 repetitions, one process per run).
claimed_speedup: vs RapidJSON: 1.4-4.6x faster reads, 2.6-8.1x faster writes across the ten documents (per-document ranges from the root README table); time-weighted totals: 2.31x faster reads, 3.91x faster writes (docs/benchmark page). vs simdjson: 1.1-1.6x faster reads against On Demand on read-only input including copy+pad (root README range); the weighted 2.14x is against simdjson DOM, and against On Demand on a caller-prepared padded buffer the weighted margin is 1.34x fresh / 1.19x with parser and allocator reused (simdjson has no serializer). vs nlohmann-json: 2.8-27x faster writes, weighted 6.67x (not in read comparison). vs upstream yyjson: 1.0-1.8x faster reads / 1.0-2.1x faster writes, weighted 1.69x / 1.46x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 15.2.0; all four benchmark executables built with -O3, -march=x86-64-v3 and link-time optimization (rapidjson and nlohmann-json are header-only and compiled with identical flags; simdjson and yyjson are prebuilt vcpkg libraries built without -march=x86-64-v3 or LTO).
hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K, 8 logical CPUs (E-cores and Turbo Boost disabled), Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, Linux 7.0.0
tradeoffs: Requires a C++20 compiler with range support; bundled backend compiles yyjson.c from source (an external-yyjson mode is also available); the huge-page allocator optimization only applies on Linux/glibc for blocks >=32MB, so most of the weighted-average gain against yyjson/simdjson on the two largest documents (fgo, otfcc) comes from that platform-specific effect rather than parsing algorithm differences; simdjson has no serializer so is excluded from write comparisons and nlohmann-json is excluded from read comparisons.

The page also says much of the weighted total comes from the bundled backend's madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) on >32 MiB blocks (Linux/glibc only), which only the two large documents (fgo, otfcc) get; with the allocator reused the fgo/otfcc read margin over yyjson shrinks to 91%/96% of its time. The per-document ranges come from the root README table; the weighted totals come from docs/benchmark/README.md. I recomputed both from the committed raw logs and they match. name: Jansson
workload: nativejson-benchmark: parse three JSON files (canada.json 2199 KB, citm_catalog.json 1737 KB, twitter.json 632 KB) into each library's DOM, and stringify the DOM back to JSON; total time over the three files.
claimed_speedup: No claim by the project; figures are from the independent suite's committed sample CSV (Jansson v2.7). Stringify total 69.9 ms vs JsonCpp 94.3 ms (1.35x) and Nlohmann 87.7 ms (1.25x), ratios derived from page data; Jansson is faster on each file (canada 64.2 vs JsonCpp 84.4 / Nlohmann 76.3 ms; citm 3.76 vs 5.68 / 7.18 ms; twitter 1.93 vs 4.14 / 4.24 ms). Parse total 112.1 ms vs JsonCpp 165.5 ms (1.48x derived) and json-c 134.6 ms (1.20x derived), but that rests on canada.json (78.5 vs JsonCpp 142.5 ms); Jansson is slower than JsonCpp on citm (22.7 vs 14.6 ms) and twitter (10.9 vs 8.5 ms) and slower than Nlohmann 2.0.3 on parse (72.5 ms total).
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS (README sample results, updated 2016-9-9); premake5 gmake build (build/premake.sh) in release configuration: optimize Full, NDEBUG, -march=native (build/premake5.lua)
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Intel Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80GHz
tradeoffs: Mutable, reference-counted tree: every node is individually allocated (224,392 allocations for canada.json, 111,230 for citm_catalog.json, 43,822 for twitter.json in the CSV), strings are copied and object entries are kept in a hashtable (ludocode benchmark reports key reordering); in return it supports editing and re-encoding documents, full UTF-8 handling, detailed error positions and a stable C API with no dependencies.
caveats: Jansson makes no speed claim; this is a derived win in an independent suite. Results are from 2016 with Jansson v2.7 and JsonCpp 1.0.0 (current releases are far newer), on one macOS machine. caveats: Number handling is loose: the parser builds a double as integer part + fraction / pow(10, digits), then multiplies by pow(10, exponent) (same code at the pinned 7053321 and at HEAD), so values are not correctly rounded (37 of 66 double-parse conformance tests pass vs 66 of 66 for Nlohmann), and the parse win over Nlohmann exists only on the double-heavy canada.json; on the other two files it is about 5% slower. Output rows are produced by udp/json-builder, a separate repository, which formats doubles with "%g" (6 significant digits, still so at HEAD): canada.json's 17-digit coordinates are truncated, so those stringify/prettify timings measure lossy output (22 of 27 roundtrip tests pass). The benchmark wrapper's own comment says stringify is 'Very slow in the current version'. Third-party suite by the RapidJSON author (disclosed in its README), sample numbers from 2016-09-09; Library versions come from the suite README's table, which was edited after the 2016-09-09 sample run (it lists cJSON 1.5.0, released 2017-05-02), so the exact versions measured are not certain. Conformance: 26 of 34 parse-validation, 37 of 66 double-parse, 9 of 9 string, 22 of 27 roundtrip (Nlohmann 34/34, 66/66, 9/9, 23/27). RapidJSON parses the three files in 7.932 ms. The project README gives no performance numbers, only design claims (never recurses, allocates only what it needs). September 2026 commits fixed parser correctness edge cases (rejection of long floats #178, overflow handling, UTF-16 surrogate pairs); the benchmark files exercise none of them (canada.json parsed, no \u escapes in citm_catalog.json or twitter.json), so the 2016 numbers are not capped by them. The repository now lives at github.com/json-parser/json-parser (udp/json-parser redirects there). Flags come from the repo's premake file, not from the result file.

name: json.h
baseline: nlohmann/json (C++11, v2.0.3 as pinned by nativejson-benchmark); the same table also has JsonCpp 1.0.0, Jansson and cJSON
workload: Parse of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json from an in-memory buffer into a DOM, time in ms. Because json.h keeps numbers as text, the harness (src/tests/sheredomjsonhtest.cpp) walks the tree after json_parse and calls atof() on every number with the result discarded; stringify times json_write_minified plus an emulation walk that sprintf's into a discarded local buffer.
claimed_speedup: Parse time in ms, json.h vs nlohmann v2.0.3: canada.json 9.418 vs 55.591 (5.9x), citm_catalog.json 5.077 vs 9.875 (1.9x), twitter.json 2.351 vs 7.010 (3.0x); three-file total 16.846 vs 72.476 ms (4.3x) (ratios derived from page data). Also parses faster than JsonCpp (142.458 / 14.587 / 8.477 ms), Jansson (78.465 / 22.656 / 10.935 ms) and cJSON (15.574 / 5.580 / 3.517 ms). Stringify json.h vs nlohmann: canada.json 29.355 vs 76.315 ms (2.6x), citm_catalog.json 4.034 vs 7.178 ms (1.8x), twitter.json 0.978 vs 4.239 ms (4.3x) (ratios derived from page data). RapidJSON is still faster than json.h (4.755 / 1.950 / 1.227 ms parse).
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit (README: 'MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015, Corei7-4980HQ@2.80GHz) with clang 7.0 64-bit', also in the result file name); build/premake5.lua release configuration uses optimize "Full" plus buildoptions -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80GHz, MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), macOS 64-bit (README and result file name)
tradeoffs: Read-only DOM in one allocation (2 allocations in the benchmark), non-streaming, numbers kept as unparsed strings so callers convert them. Memory is large on number-heavy input: canada.json 18,010,128 bytes vs nlohmann 5,293,488 (3.4x, derived from page data). The same suite's conformance table records 9 failed parse-validation cases and 7 of 9 failed string-parse cases for json.h (nlohmann passes all of both), so it accepts some invalid JSON and does not decode some string escapes in that vendored version.
caveats: Numbers are the independent nativejson-benchmark sample run (README 'Update on: 2016-9-9') on a 2014-era CPU with clang 7.0, a 2016-era json.h and nlohmann v2.0.3; nlohmann/json has been reworked since. The measured json.h did less work than the baselines: in the same suite's sample/conformance.csv it failed 9/34 parse-validation tests (pass01 rejected; fail02, fail07, fail08, fail10, fail25 raw tab, fail27 raw newline, fail29, fail30 accepted) and 7/9 string tests (string03-string09, consistent with not decoding \u escapes), while nlohmann passed all validation and string tests. Current json.h decodes \u escapes and gained fixes in 2026 (reject numbers with no digits after a sign, 2026-10-01; reject raw control characters in quoted strings, 2026-10-02; comment after a number, 2026-10-06), so the measured parser was more permissive and today's ratios may differ. json.h does not convert numbers to doubles; the harness's emulation calls atof() and discards the result, which the compiler may drop, so number conversion cost (large on canada.json) may not have been paid at all; the stringify emulation memcpy's the number payload pointer as a double and formats it into a discarded buffer, and json.h's writer copies number text verbatim with no double-to-string work. The json.h README makes no speed claim and links no benchmark; the win is a derived comparison between rows of a third-party shootout (the suite author also wrote RapidJSON, which beats json.h). Public-domain dedication (Unlicense), no patent grant. [retier] nativejson-benchmark 2016 run (clang 7.0, i7-4980HQ): the adapter sheredomjsonhtest.cpp calls atof() in ParseNumbers and discards the result, which LLVM 3.7 marks nounwind+readonly and deletes, so the canada.json parse very likely did no number conversion while nlohmann did (not confirmed by disassembly); WriteNumbers memcpy's the char* of json_number_s into a double, so stringify rows formatted pointer bits rather than document numbers. The measured build failed 9 of 34 validation tests and 7 of 9 string tests (conformance.csv), fixed later (\u decoding added, raw control characters rejected 2026-10-02). nlohmann v2.0.3 baseline from 2016. More than 15 closed issues report heap OOB, OOB reads and stack overflows (2022 to 2026-10-01, #132).

name: Jsonifier
workload: Read (parse into typed C++ structs, with UTF-8 validation on for all libraries) throughput against simdjson ondemand. Glaze is the only library compared on write. Tests: small-value files where each value is parsed as a separate tiny document (Double/Uint64/Int64/Bool/String), plus whole documents (Twitter, CitmCatalog, Canada, Discord, Google Maps, Instruments, Marine IK, Mesh, Random, minified and prettified). Measured by the adaptive-sampling BenchmarkSuite harness (commit 49d7727), pinned to Jsonifier 9b1cd1d, Glaze 76db773 and simdjson 6913ee1
claimed_speedup: Small-value tests. Each value in the file is parsed as its own tiny document (e.g. [START]true[END]). Double Test Read: 1345.06 vs simdjson 270.869 MB/s (~5.0x). Bool Test Read: 3090.41 vs 225.22 MB/s (~13.7x). String Test Read: 3881.15 vs 1591.5 MB/s (~2.4x). Uint64 Test Read: 2221.44 vs 637.965 MB/s (~3.5x). Whole-document reads are closer. Twitter (Minified): 2115.62 vs 1212.07 MB/s (~1.75x). CitmCatalog (Minified): 1816.6 vs 1050.96 MB/s (~1.73x). Canada (Minified): 866.14 vs 633.802 MB/s (~1.37x). The page marks Twitter, Google Maps and Random (Prettified) as statistical ties with simdjson. Jsonifier loses Mesh (Prettified): 1918.85 vs simdjson 2113.31 MB/s (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Clang 24.0.0, Release. From Json-Performance CMakeLists.txt: -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fomit-frame-pointer -flto=thin -finline-functions -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, linked with lld (-Wl,-O2 --gc-sections). simdjson is built with SIMDJSON_DEVELOPMENT_CHECKS OFF and UTF-8 validation on. Jsonifier uses its AVX2 backend and simdjson uses haswell
hardware: Intel Core i9-14900KF (the page prints 'i9-14900KF-AVX2'), running under WSL2 (Linux 6.18.40.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2)
tradeoffs: Requires C++20; compile-time reflection via member-pointer registration (no macros/codegen); ARM SVE2 backend explicitly marked experimental with known incorrect cases; NEON recommended for production ARM
caveats: Run and published by the Jsonifier authors in their companion repo (Json-Performance), not by an independent party. The largest gains vs simdjson (5-14x) come from small-value tests that parse thousands of tiny single-value documents, where simdjson ondemand's per-document iterate() setup cost dominates. On whole documents the gain is ~1.1-1.8x, several tests are statistical ties, and simdjson wins Mesh (Prettified). The Marine IK Reverse tests deliberately read keys out of order, which is a known worst case for ondemand. The run was on WSL2 with a Clang 24 development snapshot and pinned to commits dated 2026-09-23, so results may shift with later commits

name: jsoniter-scala
workload: Parse /tmp/1.json and average the x/y/z coordinates. json/generate_json.rb generates the file as a pretty-printed object: 'coordinates' holds 524,288 records, each with x/y/z doubles, a 'name' string and a nested 'opts' object. The timed window, bracketed by notify start/stop, excludes process/JVM startup, file loading and a two-tiny-document self-test. It runs on the same machine and Docker image as the C++ entries.
claimed_speedup: 0.147s (Scala/jsoniter-scala) vs RapidJSON 0.154s (g++) and 0.194s (clang++) (~1.05x-1.32x faster, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Scala 3.8.4: plain `scalac` (no extra options) compiles json/json-scala/src/main/scala/JsonTest.scala against jsoniter-scala-macros_3 2.39.1 (json/json-scala/Maven.list, fetched with coursier). The classes go into a fat jar built by common/jvm/combinejars.sh (not sbt-assembly), which runs as `scala application.jar` under xtime.rb. RapidJSON (a clone of miloyip/rapidjson) builds with g++ 16.1.0 as `g++ $(COMMON_FLAGS) -std=c++23` and with clang++ 22.1.8 as `clang++ $(COMMON_FLAGS) -std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++`. COMMON_FLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk). README results are dated UPDATE: 2026-07-19.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian GNU/Linux (Docker image)
tradeoffs: JVM-only, needs code-generated codecs per-type at compile time (macro-based), not a drop-in DOM parser like RapidJSON; JVM warmup/startup cost not captured by this steady-state benchmark.
caveats: The win over RapidJSON(g++) is small: 0.147 vs 0.154 s, ~1.05x. The comparison is not like-for-like in two ways. jsoniter-scala uses a compile-time typed case-class codec that decodes only x/y/z and skips name/opts, while RapidJSON builds a full DOM. The RapidJSON rows also use its default, less precise number parsing. Against RapidJSON Precise (0.212 s g++, 0.262 s clang++), jsoniter-scala leads by ~1.44x/1.78x (derived from page data). The Scala row uses more energy than g++ RapidJSON (7.89 J vs 6.61 J) and more memory (283.94+25.62 MiB vs 113.21+123.44 MiB). JIT warm-up is only the two tiny self-test calls, so this is a single-shot run, not steady-state throughput. Several C/C++ parsers are faster on the same page: simdjson On-Demand at 0.060 s, DAW JSON Link, gason and yyjson. The suite pins jsoniter-scala 2.39.1, while the current release is v2.41.1 (2026-09-25). The workload is a single synthetic one.

Small payload (190B), EachKey: 227 vs 1,300 ns/op (~5.7x faster, derived from page data). Medium (2.4KB): EachKey 1,657 and Get 3,141 vs 9,911 ns/op (~6.0x and ~3.2x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5, Go 1.26.3, median of 5 runs; comparison libraries pinned to latest versions as of 2026-07-29
hardware: Apple M4 Max (ARM64, darwin)
tradeoffs: No reflection/struct binding by default (path-based `Get`/`EachKey`/`EachObject` API instead of Unmarshal-into-struct), so migrating from encoding/json requires rewriting access code; returns []byte slices into the original buffer rather than copies unless told otherwise.
caveats: The benchmark is first-party (the project's own repo), but the methodology (hardware, Go version, run count) is fully stated, so it is treated as Tier A. The numbers are Apple-silicon ARM64, not the x86 hardware most servers run. The comparison is not like-for-like: encoding/json fully unmarshals into a typed struct, while jsonparser scans bytes and extracts only the requested fields. The result depends on the API used: on the medium payload, Get (3,141 ns/op) is slower than gjson (2,241), easyjson (2,368) and sonic (2,703), and only EachKey (1,657) leads. On the small payload, EachObject (205 ns/op) allocates 64 B/op.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'json parser faster than' surfaced 'New JSON parser for Go: up to 9x faster than encoding/json' (buger/jsonparser); opened repo README Benchmarks section.

name: libjson (vincenthz)
workload: nativejson-benchmark serialisation of three in-memory trees (canada.json, citm_catalog.json, twitter.json) to condensed and prettified JSON strings, plus a DOM statistics traversal, libjson against nlohmann/json v2.0.3.
claimed_speedup: Against nlohmann/json v2.0.3, sum of the three files (derived from page data): Stringify 68.767 ms vs 87.732 ms (about 1.28x); per file canada.json 61.512 vs 76.315 ms, citm_catalog.json 4.067 vs 7.178 ms, twitter.json 3.188 vs 4.239 ms. These rows time a benchmark-written tree printer: numbers are formatted by the harness with sprintf("%.17g") or "%lld" (libjson does no number conversion), and false/null are printed as quoted strings, so only the canada.json row (no null or false values) produces correct output. The Prettify row (69.279 vs 130.560 ms) is not a valid comparison: the harness never calls json_print_pretty, so libjson emits the same compact text as in Stringify (same time and the same 5.24 MB) while nlohmann runs dump(4). The Statistics row (0.803 vs 2.171 ms) walks the harness's own tree, not libjson code. Parse, the only row using libjson's parser to build a tree, is slower than nlohmann: 107.172 vs 72.476 ms (about 0.68x; canada 77.479 vs 55.591, citm 20.334 vs 9.875, twitter 9.359 vs 7.010 ms); it beats JsonCpp 1.0.0 (165.522 ms, about 1.54x) and json-c 0.12.1 (134.551 ms, about 1.26x) on the totals only because of canada.json (all derived from page data). Parse memory 8.59 MB vs nlohmann 9.90 MB (derived) is the harness tree's footprint.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS (suite README: 'MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015, Corei7-4980HQ@2.80GHz) with clang 7.0 64-bit', results updated 2016-9-9); premake5 gmake build, release configuration: optimize "Full" (-O3 under gmake), NDEBUG, buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra (build/premake5.lua); libjson submodule pinned at bd0cad8 (2016-04-19, suite README lists 0.8), nlohmann v2.0.3 per the suite README table
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Intel Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80GHz, macOS 64-bit (suite README and result file name)
tradeoffs: Interruptible SAX-style (SAJ) parser and printer with no object model and no number conversion: the user supplies the tree and converts numbers. LGPL (header in json.c says version 2.1 or 3.0 only); the repo has no LICENSE file. Optional nesting and size limits, UTF-8 validation, comments, custom allocators. Build system is only meant for testing; the author recommends embedding the two source files.
caveats: Harness flaws behind the numbers (src/tests/vincenthzlibjsontest.cpp, unchanged at HEAD): libjson has 'No object model integrated' (README), so the suite builds its own tree through json_parser_dom callbacks (tree_create_structure, tree_create_data, tree_append) and prints it with its own tree_print; tree_print ignores the json_print_pretty argument and always calls json_print_raw, so the Prettify row is compact output and the 1.88x prettify figure is void; tree_print emits JSON_FALSE and JSON_NULL as JSON_STRING, so twitter.json (2446 false, 1946 null) and citm_catalog.json (1263 null) are serialised wrongly; number formatting is harness sprintf. The Statistics win measures the harness tree. Parse, the row that exercises libjson, is 1.48x slower than nlohmann/json. libjson's own SAX rows have no nlohmann baseline (SAX round-trip 30.778 ms, SAX statistics 22.478 ms, versus RapidJSON 18.143 and 6.318 ms). Conformance in the same suite: 2 of 34 parse-validation, 9 of 66 double-parse and 10 of 27 round-trip tests fail (nlohmann fails 4 of 27 round-trip). The README's 'Fast: use efficient code and small parsing tables for maximum efficiency' has no numbers. Security note: json_parser_dom's dom_push realloc'd its stack without multiplying by the element size (heap overflow past 1024 nesting levels), fixed in e03b4a9 (2018-10-06) after the 2016 run; the test files never nest that deep. Sample results are dated 2016-09-09 and use 2016 library versions (nlohmann v2.0.3); today's ratios will differ. Per-library totals are sums of the three per-file rows and are derived from page data. LGPL-2.1-only OR LGPL-3.0-only (header in json.c; no LICENSE file).
found_via: seed-record pass: awesome-cpp JSON-section entry (assignment lead), repo README had no numbers; numbers found in the miloyip/nativejson-benchmark sample results CSV

verification.tier_reason: The suite meets A methodology (public harness src/tests/vincenthzlibjsontest.cpp and src/tests/nlohmanntest.cpp, clang 7.0, premake5 optimize Full + -march=native, Core i7-4980HQ), but every libjson row that beats nlohmann/json times benchmark-written code with correctness bugs: tree_print ignores its print_func argument and always calls json_print_raw, so the Prettify row produces compact output, and it emits JSON false and null as quoted strings, so the citm_catalog.json and twitter.json Stringify output is wrong. name: libjson (xnacly)
workload: Parsing JSON of varying complexity (naive, string-escape-heavy, deeply-nested 'hard' cases) via Go micro-benchmarks, plus parsing generated 1MB-100MB JSON files as a CLI end-to-end benchmark.
claimed_speedup: 1.94x-2.43x faster in Go benchmarks (ns/op) with 2.1x-3.1x fewer allocations; 1.69x-1.81x faster wall-clock time on 1MB-100MB files
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem with default Go build flags; Go toolchain version not stated (go.mod declares only a minimum, go 1.26.4). File benchmarks: go build + hyperfine (--warmup 1 --runs 10).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X 8-Core Processor, linux/amd64 (stated in the go test output; the hyperfine file benchmark does not restate hardware)
tradeoffs: Zero-copy design mutates the input byte slice in place for string unescaping, so callers cannot reuse/read the original buffer after parsing; uses a custom JIT-cached query language instead of encoding/json's reflection-based struct tags, so migration requires API changes; very new, low-adoption project.
caveats: Very small project (5 stars, single author). The 'Naive'/'Escaped'/'Hard' inputs are self-defined strings repeated inside json_test.go, not a standard external corpus. No Go toolchain version is stated. libjson mutates its input buffer for zero-copy parsing, while encoding/json unmarshals into `any` without that trade-off. The hyperfine file benchmark does not restate the machine.

name: LJSON
workload: Single-shot, millisecond-resolution DOM parse and formatted/unformatted print timings on nativejson-benchmark files (canada, twitter, citm_catalog) and author-built concatenations (twitter x10/x100/x1000, canada x100, citm x1000). The best of LJSON's 7 modes (reuse and fast arena modes) is compared with RapidJSON's default Document::Parse plus Writer/PrettyWriter, and with cJSON and yyjson
claimed_speedup: README headline figures are best-case single files ('最快可达' = 'up to' in README_zh-cn): 'parses 131% faster and prints 147% faster than RapidJSON' on Cortex-A53 (twitter.jsonx10: RapidJSON parse 178 vs LJSON reuse mode 77 ms, unformatted print 109 vs 44 ms); 'parses 75% faster and prints 133% faster' on i7-10700 (twitter.jsonx100 parse 138 vs 79 ms; canada.jsonx100 unformatted print 844 vs 362 ms). On i7-1260P the README says 'parses 166% faster and prints 215% faster' (without file I/O), but the published screenshot's best parse ratio is 1000xtwitter RapidJSON 864 vs LJSON mode 3 345 ms (~2.5x, 150% faster); the print figure matches (formatted 759 vs 241 ms, ~3.15x). On canada.json the parse gain is small: 64 vs 44 ms (A53), 477 vs 444 ms (i7-10700, x100), 333 vs 297 ms (i7-1260P, x100) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ -O2 with default options (README Note 1 and build commands; ljson is also built with -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections). gcc 14.2.0 (Debian 14.2.0-19) is shown only in the i7-1260P screenshot. Compiler versions for the Cortex-A53 and i7-10700 runs are not stated
hardware: ARM64 dev board / ARM CortexA53 (Linux-5.15); Intel i7-10700 (Ubuntu 18.04, VirtualBox); Intel i7-1260P (Debian 13, VMWare)
tradeoffs: cJSON-inspired C API; DOM/SAX dual mode with memory-pool reuse and zero-heap-allocation mode; custom ldouble float<->string codec is not fully IEEE-754 compliant (17-digit precision only) in exchange for speed
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the sole author on three of their own machines, two of them VMs, and not independently reproduced. Headline percentages are best-case files with LJSON's best arena/reuse mode. The Chinese README says 'up to', but the English README drops it. The i7-1260P parse figure (166%) could not be reproduced from its screenshot, where the best visible figure is ~150%. Timings are single runs at ms resolution. RapidJSON is built with default options (no SSE4.2/NEON, not in-situ). The 'with file reading and writing' label on the A53/i7-10700 claims does not fit the matching rows, which exclude file I/O. name: metal-json
workload: Parse-to-tape plus an identical stats walk (node count, unescaped string bytes, XOR of number payloads) inside the timed region, for both metal-json (Metal GPU kernels) and C++ simdjson's DOM tape API. The inputs are canonical twitter/citm_catalog/canada from simdjson-data plus deterministic twitter-template expansions from 1 MiB to 512 MiB. An untimed check asserts bit-identical stats before timing.
claimed_speedup: On twitter-shaped documents, 1.34x-2.71x faster than C++ simdjson from 8 MiB to 512 MiB (1.34x at 8 MiB, 1.81x at 16 MiB, 2.28x at 64 MiB, 2.06x/2.19x/2.71x at 100/256/512 MiB; 7.51 vs 2.77 GB/s at 512 MiB). On number-dense canada.json it is 1.42x faster at 2.1 MiB. It loses below the ~4.3 MiB twitter crossover: 0.96x at 4 MiB, 0.33x at 1 MiB, 0.12x (simdjson ~8x faster) at 0.6 MiB, and 0.44x on citm_catalog (1.6 MiB).
compiler_and_flags: simdjson v4.6.4 amalgamation built through the Rust cc crate with -O3 -std=c++17 -DNDEBUG and -mcpu=native on aarch64 (bench/build.rs). The C++ compiler and its version are not stated. metal-json: rustc 1.95.0 and Apple Metal toolchain 32023.883 (per bench-report.md). Criterion medians.
hardware: Apple M5 Max, 128 GiB unified memory, macOS 26.5.1
tradeoffs: GPU dispatch/sync overhead makes it far slower than simdjson on small documents; Apple Silicon/Metal + unified-memory specific, not portable to other GPUs or discrete-GPU systems; adds a GPU dependency and complexity a pure-CPU parser doesn't need.
caveats: Single machine and single vendor (one Apple M5 Max; the library runs only on Apple Silicon Metal). All rows of 1 MiB and above are expansions of the twitter template. canada and citm_catalog were measured only at their 1.6-2.1 MiB canonical sizes, so the 100-512 MiB wins cover twitter-shaped data only. The crossover (~4.3 MiB) depends on document shape and machine: canada already wins at 2.1 MiB, while citm_catalog still favors simdjson at 1.6 MiB. The timed work is a full DOM parse to tape plus a shallow stats walk on both sides. simdjson On-Demand was deliberately not compared. The C++ compiler version for the simdjson build is not stated. The project is young and small: first commit 2026-06-11, the benchmark report dated 2026-06-12, 54 commits, 18 stars. The README says 'MIT OR Apache-2.0', but the LICENSE file and Cargo.toml say MIT only.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "faster than simdjson" -> Brooooooklyn/metal-json docs/parsing-json-on-an-apple-gpu.md

The code is public (bench/benches/compare.rs, bench/src/lib.rs, bench/cpp/shim.cpp, bench/build.rs, driven by `cargo run -p xtask -- bench-report`), and the report gives the CPU (Apple M5 Max), rustc 1.95.0, the Metal toolchain version and the baseline flags (-O3, C++17, NDEBUG, -mcpu=native). But the C++ compiler that built the simdjson baseline is never named or versioned (only 'cc -O3', meaning the Rust cc crate's system default). By the same rule as simdxml (wave 4) and the Go toolchain retier, that is C, one fact short of A.

The record's caveats had two errors: 'stage-1/tape build only' is wrong, since both sides do a full DOM parse to tape plus a stats walk, and 'first commits this month' is wrong, since the first commit is 2026-06-11. name: Parson
workload: nativejson-benchmark parse of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json into each library's DOM, Parson against JsonCpp, json-c and Qt QJsonDocument (and nlohmann/json v2.0.3 as the faster reference).
claimed_speedup: Parse, sum of the three files (derived from page data): Parson 89.549 ms vs JsonCpp 1.0.0 165.522 ms (about 1.85x), json-c 0.12.1 134.551 ms (about 1.50x) and Qt 5.6 QJsonDocument 124.957 ms (about 1.40x). The win is driven by canada.json (64.573 ms vs JsonCpp 142.458, json-c 105.784, Qt 114.775); on citm_catalog.json Parson (17.144 ms) is slower than JsonCpp (14.587) and Qt (7.052) and faster than json-c (21.122); on twitter.json (7.832 ms) it is faster than JsonCpp (8.477) and slower than json-c (7.645) and Qt (3.130). Parse memory 9.14 MB vs JsonCpp 24.56 MB and json-c 49.89 MB (derived; Qt allocations are not tracked), though Parson makes more allocations (594,122 vs JsonCpp 386,181). Stringify 110.903 ms is slower than nlohmann/json v2.0.3 (87.732), JsonCpp (94.261) and json-c (30.804) and faster only than Qt (152.185, about 1.37x, derived). There is no valid prettify comparison: the suite's Parson Prettify calls json_serialize_to_string (compact), so its 111.205 ms is not comparable with nlohmann's dump(4) 130.560 ms. Parse is slower than nlohmann/json (72.476 ms), cJSON (24.671) and RapidJSON (7.932).
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS (suite README: 'MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015, Corei7-4980HQ@2.80GHz) with clang 7.0 64-bit', results updated 2016-9-9); premake5 gmake build, release configuration: optimize "Full" (-O3 under gmake), NDEBUG, buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra (build/premake5.lua); Parson revision not stated in the suite README (submodule pinned at c22be79 at HEAD), JsonCpp 1.0.0, json-c 0.12.1, Qt 5.6.1-1, nlohmann v2.0.3 per the suite README table

name: pikkr
workload: Extract 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 named fields (via JSONPath-like queries, e.g. $._id.$oid) from a 1GB generated JSON file (repeated 'companies.json' startup-company dataset) using AVX2-accelerated speculative parsing, compared against serde_json and the `json` crate.
claimed_speedup: 1 field ($._id.$oid): pikkr 954.1471 MB/s (basic parsing only) and 1424.6397 MB/s (speculative, train_num=100) vs serde_json 452.4017 MB/s (~2.1x / ~3.1x); 16 fields: pikkr 815.7086 MB/s (basic) and 966.4520 MB/s (speculative) vs serde_json 231.7726 MB/s (~3.5x / ~4.2x). MB/s values verbatim from benchmark README output; ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.22.0-nightly (d93036a04 2017-09-07), cargo 0.23.0-nightly (34c0674a2 2017-09-01) per pikkr README; bench.sh builds with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release; serde_json 1.0.3, json 0.11.9, pikkr 0.16.0 (Cargo.lock)
hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel Core i7 3.3 GHz, 1 processor / 2 cores, 256 KB L2 per core, 4 MB L3, 16 GB RAM (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Not a general-purpose DOM parser: implements the Mison 'speculative parsing' algorithm which only extracts a fixed, known set of field paths from records with a stable/repetitive structure, falling back to slow-path parsing when the structure varies; requires Rust nightly and an AVX2 CPU.
caveats: Abandoned since 2017-09-21 (no commits in ~9 years); requires nightly Rust and an AVX2 CPU, and the 2017 nightly code may not build with current rustc. First-party benchmark on a single dataset (companies.json concatenated 14x, ~1.09 GB, 263,214 records) whose uniform record structure suits pikkr's Mison-style speculative parsing; the peak numbers need training (train_num=100). The serde_json side is a hand-written DeserializeSeed query extractor that skips unneeded values with IgnoredAny, against serde_json 1.0.3 (2017); current serde_json was not tested. No exact CPU model is given.
found_via: GitHub search 'topic:json-parser --sort stars' surfaced pikkr/pikkr; opened its Performance section and linked pikkr/rust-json-parser-benchmark repo for raw numbers.

Its results are 115.2 vs 104.3 MB/s at 8 threads (~1.10x), 50.6 vs 48.0 MB/s at 1 thread (~1.05x), and ~1.01x at 2 and 4 threads. serde_json is slightly ahead in its Bun 8-worker FFI pool (124.5 vs 123.0 MB/s). simd-json's own README has only a qualitative performance claim and no numbers. Good results need AVX2/SSE4.2/NEON, and the parser mutates its input buffer.
