name: simdjson-oxcaml (simdjson-ox)
workload: Geometric-mean parse throughput (MB/s) across 7 standard JSON corpus fixtures (apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, gsoc-2018, marine_ik, numbers, twitter.json), single P-core pinned, Bechamel/Google Benchmark harness
claimed_speedup: simdjson-ox-tape-reusable (reusable tape parser) geomean 1247.7 MB/s vs rapidjson-dom 1059.7 MB/s (~1.18x, derived from page data; README states 118% of RapidJSON) and vs nlohmann-json-dom 132.2 MB/s (~9.4x, derived from page data). Per fixture the tape-reusable mode beats RapidJSON on apache_builds (1555 vs 867 MB/s), citm_catalog (2072 vs 1649), gsoc-2018 (2257 vs 1092) and twitter (1428 vs 1048) but is slower on canada (759 vs 990), marine_ik (668 vs 885) and numbers (894 vs 1047). The recommended DOM API is slower than RapidJSON: simdjson-ox-reusable 729.5 MB/s and one-shot simdjson-ox 659.4 MB/s geomean (README: 69% of RapidJSON). Still behind C++ simdjson-dom (3344.5 MB/s) and sajson-dom (1650.9 MB/s).
compiler_and_flags: OCaml 'perf' dune profile (native flags -g, -gno-upstream-dwarf, -gdwarf-inlined-frames, -gdwarf-fidelity high) on OxCaml 5.2.0+ox / Dune 3.22.2; C++ comparators (RapidJSON, nlohmann, sajson, simdjson) built with GCC 15.2.1, CMake Release config
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700K (8 P-core + 4 E-core, 20 logical CPUs), pinned to logical CPU 0 (P-core) via taskset, performance governor, ASLR disabled, Fedora Linux 43, kernel 6.19.14-200.fc43.x86_64
tradeoffs: Still ~2.7x slower than C++ simdjson-dom and ~1.3x slower than sajson-dom in the same run; OCaml GC allocates significant minor/major words per parse (reported in the table) unlike the zero/near-zero-alloc C++ parsers; SIMD path is currently x86-oriented (SSE/AVX via ocaml_simd), no ARM NEON yet; error reporting is described by the author as still rudimentary; only the 'tape-reusable' variant beats RapidJSON — the plain simdjson-ox and non-reusable tape variants sit at or below RapidJSON's geomean.
caveats: The win over RapidJSON comes only from the lower-level tape mode with a reusable parser (zero OCaml allocation in the loop), while the RapidJSON harness builds a fresh rapidjson::Document every iteration. The author says tape vs DOM APIs 'are not identical enough for a strictly like-for-like comparison'. The recommended DOM API is about 0.69x RapidJSON, and tape mode loses to RapidJSON on 3 of 7 fixtures (canada, marine_ik, numbers). The author labels it a single-run, point-in-time snapshot (turbo on, frequency not locked). x86-only SIMD. Very new project with 3 stars.

Untyped twitter serialize: 390.00 us vs serde_json 797.34 us (~2.0x) and simd_json 981.14 us (~2.5x). serde_json is slightly faster on canada serialization: 6.5747 vs 6.7082 ms untyped and 4.6281 vs 4.7481 ms struct.

name: zenjson
workload: Parsing and stringifying the nativejson-benchmark corpus (twitter.json, canada.json, citm_catalog.json).
claimed_speedup: Parsing (derived from page data): 1.81x-3.57x faster than RapidJSON (twitter.json 2034.7 vs 570.3 MB/s = 3.57x; canada.json 3.048 vs 5.509 ms = 1.81x; citm_catalog.json 0.715 vs 1.869 ms = 2.61x). 13.8x-26.7x faster than nlohmann/json. Slightly slower than simdjson on twitter and citm (by 1-3%), and simdjson is 1.46x faster on canada. Stringifying (derived from page data): 2.64x-4.25x faster than RapidJSON (0.712 vs 1.877 ms, 8.723 vs 24.125 ms, 0.777 vs 3.299 ms) and 7.8x-15.3x faster than nlohmann/json.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (MSVC toolset v141), 64-bit. The committed benchmark/jsonbenchmark.vcxproj Release|x64 uses MaxSpeed (/O2), IntrinsicFunctions (/Oi), WholeProgramOptimization and NDEBUG. RapidJSON uses RAPIDJSON_SSE2 and ParseInsitu. simdjson is compiled with /std:c++17 and allocate_capacity pre-allocation. The others use default settings.
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700K
tradeoffs: In-situ parsing modifies and depends on the input buffer (like RapidJSON's insitu mode), so callers lose the original string; single-header and small (<2k LOC) but unmaintained since 2019, so it lacks fixes for JSON edge cases found in the years since.
caveats: No commits since 2019-09-16 (abandoned) and only 8 stars. The benchmark ran on a single 2017-era Windows/MSVC machine, with no Linux/GCC/Clang numbers. Library versions are not stated, and the RapidJSON/simdjson/nlohmann headers are not in the repo; the simdjson row uses the 2019 ParsedJson/json_parse API. In the stringify loop, RapidJSON's StringBuffer and PrettyWriter are never cleared between the 1000 iterations, so its stringify time includes appending and regrowing an ever-larger buffer; zenjson overwrites a fixed 4 MB buffer. zenjson and RapidJSON pretty-print, while nlohmann's dump() is compact. zenjson parses in situ, mutating the input. The README does not say Release explicitly; the Release|x64 settings come from the committed .vcxproj.

name: Boost.JSON

It compares boost (default allocator) and boost (pool/monotonic_resource) against rapidjson (CrtAllocator), rapidjson (MemoryPoolAllocator) and nlohmann/json. Each configuration runs for at least 5 s per sample, and the median samples are averaged.
claimed_speedup: Page charts, in MB/s, listed as clang / gcc / msvc. Parse citm_catalog: boost 476/503/477 vs nlohmann 140/143/148 (~3.3-3.5x, derived from page data), and boost(pool) 1120/1096/999 vs rapidjson(pool) 1200/1279/978, so it is slower on clang and gcc and roughly tied on msvc. Parse canada: boost 385/395/369 vs nlohmann 55/26/52 (~7-15x, derived from page data), and boost(pool) 642/675/637 vs rapidjson(pool) 506/641/490. Serialize citm_catalog: boost 2882/3263/2128 vs nlohmann 1151/1204/1142 (~1.9-2.7x, derived from page data) and vs rapidjson 2210/2469/2135. Across all 14 files x 3 compilers (derived from page data / bench/results.txt): boost beats nlohmann in 42/42 parse cases (2.1x-38.7x, median ~2.6x) and 42/42 serialize cases (1.7x-9.3x, median ~3.5x). Against RapidJSON, boost (default) wins only 20/42 parse cases (median ~0.94x); boost(pool) beats rapidjson(pool) in 33/42 parse cases (median ~1.26x); boost beats rapidjson in 33/42 serialize cases (median ~1.17x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.1 (-O3), clang 12.0 (-O3), msvc 19.26 (/O2); x64/sse2 builds
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700K CPU @ 4.20GHz, Windows 10, 32GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 479 stars on the standalone mirror (Boost.JSON ships as part of the wider Boost distribution, so GitHub stars understate real usage)
tradeoffs: Requires (or vendors) the wider Boost dependency footprint even though Boost.JSON itself is usable header-only/standalone; API is more verbose than nlohmann's for simple use cases; memory footprint (502MB/621MB in this test) sits between RapidJSON and yyjson.
caveats: These are first-party results, last regenerated on 2020-10-21 (commit 8f42799) and not re-run since; bench/bench.cpp has changed since then (2025 commits). The RapidJSON and nlohmann versions are unpinned (bench/clone.sh does a depth-1 clone of HEAD) and are not stated on the page. name: ffjson
workload: Marshal/unmarshal of a Cloudflare log-line struct (goser benchmark) and a Stripe-Customer-like nested struct (go.stripe benchmark) using Go benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: 1.91x faster than encoding/json on the goser benchmark; 2.11x faster than encoding/json on the go.stripe benchmark
tradeoffs: Requires a code-generation step (the ffjson tool generates MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON per struct) instead of runtime reflection, adding a build step and generated-code maintenance burden; larger binary size from generated code.
caveats: The README says only '2x to 3x' faster than encoding/json. It gives no results table, Go version, or hardware. Benchmark code does exist: tests/goser and tests/go.stripe each have BenchmarkMarshalJSON/BenchmarkFFMarshalJSON/BenchmarkUnmarshalJSON/BenchmarkFFUnmarshalJSON, run by 'make bench'. The 2014 launch blog post gives 1.91x (goser) and 2.11x (go.stripe) for Marshal only, because Unmarshal did not exist yet. It states no Go version or hardware. A third-party table in the easyjson README (go1.6, Feb 2016, no CPU stated) measures ffjson against encoding/json. Unmarshal: 66 vs 22 MB/s regular (~3.0x) and 17.6 vs 9.7 MB/s small (~1.8x). Marshal: 122 vs 75 (~1.6x), 36 vs 32 (~1.1x) and 134 vs 80 MB/s large (~1.7x). Those ratios are derived from page data, so marshal gains were below the README's 2-3x there. ffjson falls back to encoding/json for interface members, custom marshalers, complex map values, and some nested slices/inline structs. The README warns that with interfaces it 'may even become slower than using json.Marshal directly'. The last commit on master is 2019-09-30 (repo pushed_at 2023-09-21 has no matching commit on any branch), so all numbers predate many encoding/json improvements.

name: jbson
workload: JSON text parsing: mloskot/json_benchmark (1000 iterations of 500 small documents, and 1000 iterations of canada.json as one large document) and sanSS/json-bechmarks (small, medium and large objects, average time per parse and memory), jbson parsing JSON into its BSON document.
claimed_speedup: json_benchmark, README figures: large 43.0072 to 43.0377 s vs jsoncpp 62.7781 to 62.7823 s (1.46x), QJsonDocument 58.1027 to 58.1235 s (1.35x), jsoncons 243.634 to 243.796 s (5.7x); small 1.24328 to 1.27775 s vs jsoncpp 2.4124 to 2.45696 s (about 1.9x) and jsoncons 10.2386 to 10.2747 s (8x), ratios derived from page data. sanSS benchmark: medium 64,800 us vs jsoncpp 121,035 us and QJsonDocument 82,839 us; large 190,883 us vs jsoncpp 438,745 us (QJsonDocument did not finish); memory 24,708 K vs jsoncpp 44,224 K on medium objects and 1,132 K vs 4,084 K on small. README: 'it's 2nd only to rapidjson (or 3rd to QJsonDocument with small input)'.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++14 library whose JSON parser emits a BSON-style byte document that is read lazily through iterators and constant wrappers, not an in-memory DOM; BSON names cannot hold NUL so JSON compliance is partial; the README says it needs a current libc++ (codecvt and C++14 aliases missing from older libstdc++).
caveats: First-party run: the README gives the author's own timings with no compiler, flags, hardware or library versions, so tier C even though mloskot/json_benchmark is public (its own README lists no jbson or jsoncons row and shows different absolute times on other hardware); the jbson benchmark adapters are not published anywhere found (no bench directory in the repo). It is slower than RapidJSON (small 0.454 to 0.486 s, large 4.857 to 4.863 s, so about 9x on large) and, on small input, slower than QJsonDocument (1.046 to 1.056 s). json_reader parses straight into a BSON byte buffer that is then read through iterators, a different data model from the DOMs it is compared with. README's large-object memory figure is garbled ('70,7748 K'). README says the library is known to work only with an up-to-date libc++. 2015 numbers, repository last changed 2015-12-20. Both benchmark repos are unmaintained or superseded by nativejson-benchmark, which has no jbson row.

name: jist
workload: Extracting a single key-path value (the last array element) from large synthetic JSON array files (3.3GB via the simdjson path; 28.9GB via the streaming lexer fallback)
claimed_speedup: 3.3GB file (get last element): jist 2.05s vs jq 34.17s (~16.7x, derived from page data), 1600MB/s vs 96MB/s, 4.5GB vs 18GB memory. 28.9GB file: jist 1:30s, 9.7MB memory, 321MB/s (streaming json-tools fallback); jq could not run ('not enough ram').
compiler_and_flags: Both jist and the Rust data generator are built with 'cargo build --release' (the README marks building jist from source as optional). build.rs compiles the vendored simdjson with only -std=c++17 added, and neither the Rust nor the C++ compiler version is stated.
hardware: Intel i7-12700H, 64GB DDR5@4800MT RAM
tradeoffs: Uses simdjson internally (does not itself beat simdjson) and falls back to a much slower (~300MB/s) character-based lexer for files >4.2GB or forced streaming mode; jq has vastly broader query capability than jist's single key-path extraction
caveats: jist itself is a Rust CLI (~63KB of Rust) that calls a vendored simdjson (the source of GitHub's 'C++' language label) through autocxx/cxx. The C++ speed comes from simdjson, and the 28.9GB streaming run uses the Rust json-tools lexer, not simdjson. The benchmark is first-party: one synthetic data shape, one query, compared only with jq (a C tool), not with simdjson, RapidJSON or nlohmann directly. The generator is public but the jq invocation and timing method are not scripted, and compiler versions and flags are not documented.

name: JsonFusion
workload: Six realistic parse+validate+populate scenarios (embedded config static/dynamic, telemetry samples, RPC commands, log events, bus events, metrics/time-series), 1M iterations each; separately, twitter.json (0.6 MB, 100 status objects) parse+populate+validate benchmark comparing full C++ library workflows.
claimed_speedup: vs RapidJSON + manual mapping (parse+validate+populate): ~same speed on static embedded config (vs hand-written SAX), 40% faster dynamic embedded config, 20% faster telemetry, 65% faster RPC commands, 15% faster log events, 20% faster bus events, 15% faster metrics; about 1.5x faster on twitter.json (1020 vs 1620 microseconds/iter). On canada.json it is ~15% slower than RapidJSON for parse-and-populate and ~80% slower than hand-written RapidJSON SAX for typed streaming; only with selective field-skipping (float parsing skipped) is it ~60% faster than hand-written RapidJSON SAX.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14 (6-scenario benchmark), GCC 14.3 (twitter.json benchmark); canada.json compiler not stated. The README states no optimization flags or build type. The repo CMakeLists.txt adds -flto=8 -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections (plus -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti on the synthetic and canada targets) only in the Release config.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, macOS 26.1 (6-scenario benchmark); arm64 Ubuntu Linux 24.04 machine, CPU model not stated (twitter.json benchmark); canada.json hardware not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only C++23 reflection-based parser (uses Boost.PFR); no SIMD, no hand-tuned assembly by design; forward-only-iterator streaming API differs from DOM-based RapidJSON; default floating-point backend does not guarantee perfect round-trip precision; ~3x slower than Glaze and ~15% slower than RapidJSON on canada.json parse-and-populate; on 8-bit AVR its code size (25.8KB) is larger than jsmn/cJSON.
caveats: First-party README benchmark. The CPU model is given for one table only (M1 Max), and neither table gives optimization flags or build type, so methodology is only partly specified. Mixed results: on canada.json it is ~15% slower than RapidJSON parse+populate and ~80% slower than RapidJSON SAX in typed streaming, and the ~60% win needs skip annotations that avoid float parsing entirely, so it is not equal work. The README says Glaze is ~3x faster on twitter.json. The README's benchmark links (benchmarks/main.cpp, benchmarks/canada_json_parsing.cpp) are stale; the code now lives in benchmarks/syntetic/ and benchmarks/canada_json/. A very young, low-star project, recently added to vcpkg; the numbers are self-reported and have not been reproduced independently.

name: libdart
baseline: nlohmann/json (version not stated); the same run also has RapidJSON, sajson, YAJL and Jansson
workload: Google Benchmark run (benchmark/configurable.cc) over the repo's benchmark/input.json (newline-separated JSON packets): parse each packet to a DOM (Dart from_json, which in this build tokenizes with sajson and then lowers into Dart's sorted finalized buffer or dynamic heap), key lookups on pre-parsed results, and serialize back to a string.
claimed_speedup: Single-run table, ns per pass over the input: Dart finalized parse 27682 vs nlohmann 254695 (9.2x), Dart dynamic parse 158967 vs nlohmann 254695 (1.6x), Dart key lookups 3803 vs 8471 (2.2x), Dart finalized serialize 36241 vs nlohmann 68175 (1.9x), Dart dynamic serialize 43105 vs 68175 (1.6x) (ratios derived from page data). sajson parses faster than Dart (14360 ns) and RapidJSON in-situ is close (34035 ns). PARSING.md: Dart runs 'within about 50% of RapidJSON' on parse.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -DNDEBUG plus dart_default_compile_options (benchmark/CMakeLists.txt); the benchmark CMake defines DART_USE_SAJSON when sajson.h is found, which switches Dart's parser to sajson; compiler and version not stated
hardware: 'middle-end 2018 MacBook Pro'; Google Benchmark header reports 8 X 2300 MHz CPUs, L3 6291K; exact CPU model not named
tradeoffs: Object keys are stored lexicographically sorted (iteration order is stable but not insertion order); no incremental parsing; finalized packets are immutable flat buffers, mutation needs a dynamic heap form and an expensive lowering step; copy-on-write reference counting (thread-unsafe pointer used in the benchmark). Header-only C++14 interface plus an ABI-stable C89 interface. JSON parsing itself is delegated to RapidJSON or sajson, YAML to libyaml.
caveats: First-party numbers from a single run on a 2018 laptop (the doc itself calls single-run output noisy and says the graphs use 16 repetitions, which are images not text). nlohmann version (found as a system install by find_path) and compiler are not stated, so tier A is not met. Dart is not a tokenizer of its own here: the table was regenerated in commit 3d45bc0 ('Added a new, stupid-fast, sajson based parser', 2019-06-01), where Dart's from_json parses with sajson (include/dart/connector/json.tcc under DART_USE_SAJSON) and then lowers into the Dart buffer; that commit replaced the RapidJSON-backed finalized-parse figure of 66174 ns with 27682 ns. A default library build without the use_sajson option parses through RapidJSON and is slower than the quoted figure, so the 9.2x win over nlohmann mostly reflects sajson versus nlohmann; sajson alone parses in 14360 ns and the project's text says sajson is the choice for raw parse speed. The 'within about 50% of RapidJSON' sentence predates the sajson path. The key-lookup row measures lookups in Dart's sorted flat buffer on pre-parsed packets, not parse work. Dart requires lexicographically sorted object keys. The repo's LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 although the list tag said MIT. The repo was archived by the owner on Jul 16, 2024 and the last commit is 2021-09-11. [retier] First-party PARSING.md numbers; since commit 3d45bc0 (2019-06-01) the finalized parser is sajson, so the 27682 ns figure is sajson plus lowering (the RapidJSON-backed figure was 66174 ns) and the 9.2x over an unversioned nlohmann is mostly sajson's win. use_sajson is OFF by default; the benchmark CMake enables it when sajson.h is found. sajson keeps only int32 integers (larger become doubles, precision lost above 2^53) and its doubles are not correctly rounded (28/66 double tests failed in 2016); the bench input (10 packets of about 1 KB, 150 small ints, no doubles) exercises neither. Dart rows use unsafe_ptr; the key-lookup counter is mis-scaled (ns column fine); the YAJL generator writes false for true; the finalized parse allocates json.size()*8. Compiler and CPU model unstated. Archived 2024-07-16; Apache-2.0.

name: libJSON (IgnacioPomar)
workload: Read (parse + walk full DOM) and write (build DOM + serialize) of random-walk OHLC minute-candle JSON at three sizes (10, 1,440 and 10,080 candles), minimum time over 30 rounds.
claimed_speedup: Read faster than nlohmann/json at every size tested: ~1.25x (small, 21.1us vs 26.4us), ~1.42x (medium, 2632.2us vs 3737.0us), ~1.38x (large, 19772.3us vs 27254.9us) (derived from page data); loses on write, and loses to RapidJSON/simdjson/glaze on both read and write
compiler_and_flags: Not stated with the results; benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (benchmark executable C++20, libJSON built as C++17 static lib); nlohmann_json 3.12.0, rapidjson cci.20250205, simdjson 4.6.3, glaze 2.9.5 via Conan
tradeoffs: Every JSON node is its own heap allocation via shared_ptr (one make_shared per value), making it the slowest of the four libraries tested at writing; author explicitly built it as a C++17/shared_ptr learning exercise, not for production use; loses to RapidJSON, simdjson and glaze on every measured workload and only beats nlohmann/json.
caveats: Self-described learning project, solo author, 0 stars. The repo dates from 2021; the benchmarks and the vector-based containers behind the read win were added 2026-09-22. No CPU model, compiler or flags are stated for the numbers. The results table is in the root README, and the methodology and usability annex are in the Spanish benchmarks/README.md, which has no numbers. It loses on write: nlohmann/json is faster at every size (34.0 vs 21.0 us, 4,388.1 vs 3,042.3 us, 32,568.2 vs 21,225.0 us). It also loses to RapidJSON, simdjson (DOM) and glaze json_t on both read and write. The author says he would pick glaze for real use and praises RapidJSON. The win over nlohmann/json (1.25x-1.42x read) is modest. The README documents that libJSON has no public API for modifying an existing field. Unlicense public-domain dedication, so there is no patent grant.

name: metajson (iod::metajson)
workload: Encoding/decoding C++ structs and vectors whose structure is known at compile time, compared to nlohmann/json and RapidJSON
claimed_speedup: Up to 9x faster than nlohmann/json and 2x faster than RapidJSON (author states these numbers are not from a comprehensive benchmark)
compiler_and_flags: libraries/metajson/benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt builds the Google Benchmark programs with -std=c++1z -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native. The README's 'Compilers' section (GCC 7.1.1, Clang 5.0.1) lists supported compilers and does not say which one produced the 9x/2x figures.

name: Mison (speculative structural-index JSON parser)
workload: Single-threaded field-projection queries over real-world JSON loaded into memory: Twitter Q1-Q8 (records have 25-30 top-level fields and a nested user object of 37-38 fields), Yelp business records (16 top-level fields), and GitHub user records (31 fixed fields). The paper compares parsing throughput (GB/s) of Mison against Gson, Jackson and RapidJSON, each using its streaming-mode API. It also runs TPC-H queries through Spark with Mison vs Jackson.
claimed_speedup: Paper Sec 6.1.1 / Fig. 8 (Twitter, Q1-Q8, single thread, throughput in GB/s): 'Mison is between 5.5 and 9.1 times faster than the best competitor in this experiment. The best case for Mison (8~9X) is for simple queries on mandatory fields (Q1-Q4)'. RapidJSON is one of the three competitors, so Mison is at least 5.5x faster than RapidJSON on Q1-Q8 (derived from page data; in the Fig. 8 bars Jackson, not RapidJSON, is the best competitor). Sec 6.1.2 (Fig. 9, GitHub dataset, all 31 fields, no projection push-down): Mison 'still outperforms the best existing JSON parser (Jackson) by a factor of 2'. Sec 6.1.4 / Fig. 11 (Twitter, first+last field query): basic (non-speculative) Mison beats Jackson by 3.6x, speculative Mison by 10.2x.
compiler_and_flags: Mison is a C++ static library; the first structural-index step uses 256-bit AVX2 SIMD and the bit-parallel steps use 64-bit instructions. The paper does not state the compiler, its version, or the flags for Mison or RapidJSON, nor the JVM version used for Jackson and Gson.
hardware: 3.5GHz Intel Xeon E5-1620 v3 (the paper calls it 'Broadwell-EP'), 16GB DDR3, 64-bit Windows 10; single-threaded runs with the JSON data preloaded into memory (I/O excluded)
stars_or_usage: Published VLDB 2017 (PVLDB Vol. 10, No. 10, pp. 1118-1129) by Microsoft Research and University of Pittsburgh; no official source release found
tradeoffs: Requires an offline training phase to build 'pattern trees' from sample data before speculative parsing works well; benefit shrinks as the fraction of queried fields grows (Fig. 12) and for highly irregular/schema-varying JSON; only helps analytical/partial-field workloads, not full-document parse+build (Sec 6.1, 'if all fields are needed... [binary formats are] still the most efficient approach').
caveats: No official Mison source was found: the MSR publication page and the paper link no code or artifact. Only unofficial reimplementations exist, none benchmarked against the paper: pikkr/pikkr (Rust, 641 stars, MIT), ubnt-intrepid/misosoup (Rust, 9 stars), leocassarani/mison (Rust, 10 stars, no license), Anghagaed/MISON (21 stars, no license) and indiependente/gomison (Go, 0 stars). The compiler and flags are unstated, and in Fig. 8 RapidJSON (SAX/streaming API on Windows) is slower than Java's Jackson, so the C++ comparison point may not be well tuned. The paper calls the E5-1620 v3 'Broadwell-EP', but v3 Xeon E5 parts are Haswell-EP (a 2014-era CPU). The speedups rely on projection/filter push-down; when all fields are parsed the gain drops to about 2x over Jackson.
found_via: WebSearch: "Mison A Fast JSON Parser for Data Analytics VLDB rapidjson speedup pdf"; paper opened directly at vldb.org

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 10(10) 2017 paper whose Sec 6.1 benchmarks Mison against RapidJSON (plus Jackson and Gson). It reports Mison 5.5-9.1x faster than the best competitor on Twitter Q1-Q8 (Fig. 8) and states the CPU (Xeon E5-1620 v3). No code, compiler or flags are published, so it cannot be A. Under this verifier's rubric that is B, the same tier the wave-3 no-code ASPLOS paper StreamTok received.
verification.notes: I raised the tier from C to B. name: NetJSON
workload: Serialization and deserialization of a simple object (SimpleSpeedTester harness, theburningmonk 2014 JSON serializers benchmark), comparing NetJSON with Json.NET 6.0.4, ServiceStack.Text 4.0.24, Jil 1.7.0, protobuf-net, JavaScriptSerializer, DataContractJsonSerializer and others. The README's headline ratios correspond to serialization times.
claimed_speedup: README states 3.4x faster than JSON.NET, 2.4x than ServiceStack JSON, 1.8x than Jil, 6x than JSON.NET BSON, 16.5x than JavaScriptSerializer, 4.3x than DataContractJsonSerializer, 1.6x than protobuf-net. In the linked 2014 theburningmonk results table (image), these ratios match serialization times only: NetJson 112.24 ms vs Json.Net 380.59 ms (~3.39x, derived from linked table data). Deserialization gain is smaller: 175.00 ms vs 437.53 ms (~2.5x vs Json.NET, derived). In that same table protobuf-net beat NetJSON on both serialization (100.68 vs 112.24 ms) and deserialization (163.20 vs 175.00 ms). The README's 1.6x-vs-protobuf-net figure comes from its own separate log: serialization 157.99 vs 257.98 ms, deserialization about equal (252.18 vs 251.50 ms).

tradeoffs: The cited numbers come from a single 2014 third-party blog post (theburningmonk.com) built on the author's own SimpleSpeedTester harness; that page presents results as charts rather than a machine-readable table and does not state CPU/hardware or .NET runtime version; the comparison predates System.Text.Json (shipped in .NET Core 3.0), so the modern .NET default serializer was never benchmarked against it.
caveats: The README ratios are serialization-only figures from a 2014 third-party blog post whose results are images, with no CPU, .NET runtime version or build configuration disclosed. name: sajson
workload: Full in-memory parse with UTF-8 validation, single-threaded, best time. 14 files: apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc-2018, instruments, marine_ik, mesh, mesh.pretty, numbers, random, twitter, twitterescaped, update-center. sajson uses static (bounded) allocation. RapidJSON 1.1.0 runs with kParseValidateEncodingFlag in both default and insitu modes.
claimed_speedup: Paper text: "In practice, we find that another C++ parser, sajson, is faster [than RapidJSON]". Paper Table 10 (Skylake i7-6700, GCC 9.1, GB/s): sajson (static allocation) 0.62-1.2 vs RapidJSON insitu 0.41-1.0 and RapidJSON default 0.38-0.86. Examples: twitter 1.0 vs 0.72 insitu / 0.45 default; apache_builds 1.2 vs 0.80 / 0.48; canada 0.76 vs 0.43 / 0.43. Derived from page data: sajson is 1.10-1.77x faster than RapidJSON insitu (geomean ~1.4x) and 1.37-2.5x faster than RapidJSON default (geomean ~1.9x). Paper Table 9 (twitter, parse only): 1.0 vs 0.8 GB/s on Skylake and 0.9 vs 0.7 GB/s on Cannon Lake. README: "sajson's performance is excellent - it frequently benchmarks faster than RapidJSON, for example".
compiler_and_flags: Paper: GCC 9.1, -O3 -march=native, Linux, no PGO. Author blog harness (chadaustin/Web-Benchmarks json/SConstruct): -O2 -g -fno-exceptions -DNDEBUG -std=c++11 with gcc/clang (versions not stated); MSVC 14; Xcode 8.3.2.
hardware: Paper: Intel i7-6700 Skylake, 3.4 GHz base / 3.7 GHz max, hyper-threading disabled; also Intel i3-8121U Cannon Lake. Author blog chart titles: Haswell i7-4771 (Windows 7, MSVC 14 and MinGW), Broadwell i5-5200U (Ubuntu 16.04, gcc/clang), iPhone SE (Xcode 8.3.2), Atom D2700 (Ubuntu, 64-bit).
tradeoffs: In-situ parser that mutates the input buffer; no UTF-16/UTF-32 support; no 64-bit integer type; single-allocation mode requires sizing the worst-case output buffer up front
caveats: Paper numbers use sajson's static-allocation mode. In dynamic-allocation mode (0.46-1.0 GB/s) sajson is slower than RapidJSON insitu on 6 of 14 files: citm_catalog, gsoc-2018, instruments, mesh.pretty, random and update-center. Snapshots are from 2018-2019: sajson 2018-09-20 and RapidJSON 1.1.0. sajson supports only 32-bit integers, does partial UTF-8 validation (it accepts some invalid sequences) and parses in situ (it modifies the input). The author's own 2017 blog numbers are only in chart images. That blog says that with GCC, RapidJSON, sajson and pjson are 'very similar'; its large wins (about 2-3x) are with MSVC, clang and iPhone builds. The repo's own benchmark/benchmark.cpp times only sajson and does not run RapidJSON.

claimed_speedup: Vs encoding/json v1.16.2 (Go 1.16.2 stdlib), Core i9-8950HK, benchstat n=5+5: Marshal/*json.codeResponse2 6.40ms -> 3.82ms (-40.29%), Unmarshal 28.1ms -> 5.6ms (-80.21%); speed 303 -> 507 MB/s (+67.47%) marshal and 69.2 -> 349.6 MB/s (+405.42%) unmarshal (~1.68x marshal, ~5.0x unmarshal, derived from page data); Unmarshal alloc 1.80MB -> 0.02MB (-99.14%) and 76.6k -> 0.1k allocs/op (-99.92%). name: ssrJSON
workload: dumps / dumps_to_bytes / loads (str and bytes input) on twitter.json, github.json, canada.json, mesh.json and simple_object_zh.json (README charts, v0.0.17). Measured with the companion ssrjson-benchmark package (src/ssrjson_benchmark/benchmark.py): the stdlib json baseline uses separators=(',', ':'), libraries are interleaved across rounds, and the process is pinned to one core. Python 3.14, x86-64 AVX2, compared against json, ujson, pydantic_core, msgspec and orjson.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'ssrjson.dumps() is about 4x-31x as fast as json.dumps()' and 'ssrjson.loads() is about 2x-8x as fast as json.loads()' for both str and bytes input (Python3.14, x86-64, AVX2). TL;DR: 'faster than or nearly as fast as orjson ... on most benchmark cases'. The page's v0.0.17 charts label these ratios vs json. dumps to str: canada 23.07x, mesh 17.79x, github 9.63x, twitter 7.52x, simple_object_zh 4.93x. loads str: canada 7.75x, mesh 4.49x, github 3.40x, simple_object_zh 2.58x, twitter 2.54x. dumps_to_bytes: canada 26.27x. orjson on the same charts: twitter loads str 1.80x, canada dumps to str 16.67x.
compiler_and_flags: Clang is required: CMakeLists.txt aborts unless CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID is Clang, and Windows uses clang-cl. CMake defaults to Release (-fomit-frame-pointer, -fno-stack-protector; LTO/PGO optional). PyPI wheels are built by a Nix flake in .github/workflows/release.yml. The Clang version is not stated anywhere, and the benchmark reports record only the CPython build compiler.
hardware: Not stated for the README's v0.0.17 dumps/loads charts, which say only 'x86-64, AVX2'. The float-formatting micro-benchmark names Apple M1 and AMD R7-7840H. The linked ssrJSON-benchmark repo publishes per-CPU PDF reports (e.g. i7-13700K AVX2 for 0.0.21 with Python 3.14.6 built by GCC 15.3.0; also i7-11370H, Ryzen 9 9900X, Apple M1/M4, Raspberry Pi 5), but none for 0.0.17.

Both ssrJSON and orjson use a global short-key cache in loads, which the benchmark README warns may not reflect production. dumps_to_bytes results depend on the UTF-8 cache setting. Requires x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2) or aarch64, and CPython only.

name: jsmn
workload: Tokenizing 14 in-memory JSON files (twitter, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc-2018, numbers, etc.), single-threaded, best time. jsmn_parse writes into a token array sized to the input, in the default build without JSMN_PARENT_LINKS. RapidJSON and nlohmann/json do full DOM parses.
claimed_speedup: The project claim "world fastest JSON parser/tokenizer" is not supported. Paper Table 10 (Skylake i7-6700, GCC 9.1, GB/s): jsmn beats JSON for Modern C++ (nlohmann/json) on 8 of 14 files, e.g. numbers 0.65 vs 0.06, github_events 0.52 vs 0.09, twitter 0.27 vs 0.10, instruments 0.24 vs 0.10. It is slower on the other 6: canada 0.01 vs 0.05, random 0.03 vs 0.07, apache_builds 0.07 vs 0.10, mesh 0.05 vs 0.06, mesh.pretty 0.09 vs 0.11, update-center 0.06 vs 0.07. Derived from page data: geomean ~1.5x faster than nlohmann/json. Against RapidJSON (default 0.38-0.86, insitu 0.41-1.0 GB/s), jsmn is slower on 12 of 14 files. It is faster only on numbers (0.65 vs 0.45) and on github_events against the default mode (0.52 vs 0.46).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.1, -O3 -march=native, Linux (simdjson VLDB paper; simdjson v0.2.1 Makefile)
hardware: Intel i7-6700 Skylake, 3.4 GHz, hyper-threading disabled (simdjson VLDB paper)
tradeoffs: Tokenizer only (no value conversion), zero dynamic allocation, tokens are boundary pointers into the source buffer rather than a DOM; C89, no libc dependency, designed for embedded/AVR/ARM targets
caveats: jsmn is only a tokenizer. It does not convert numbers, unescape strings, validate UTF-8 or build a queryable DOM, so a comparison with DOM parsers is not like-for-like. The paper says jsmn accepts invalid JSON such as [0e+]. The paper ran the default build without JSMN_PARENT_LINKS; the author's page says that build is 'terribly slow' on large objects (canada 0.01 GB/s). In the paper jsmn is slower than RapidJSON, sajson, gason and cJSON on most files. A 2012 third-party benchmark by Lev Walkin (lionet.livejournal.com/118853.html, code vlm/vlm-json-test) reports jsmn at 16 MB/s by default and 482 MB/s with the parent-links hack, vs yajl 249 MB/s, json-c 38 MB/s and Jansson 25 MB/s; it states no hardware or compiler. The README itself has no numbers. Last commit 2021-10-14.

name: Cista++
workload: Serialize/deserialize/traverse a graph of nodes and edges (object-oriented graph with pointers/indices) using the 'offset' and 'raw' variants of Cista++, compared to cereal, Cap'n Proto, and FlatBuffers
claimed_speedup: Cista++ `offset` (slim variant) vs cereal: serialize 4 ms vs 216 ms, deserialize 0.16 ms vs 111.00 ms, deserialize & traverse 66 ms vs 174 ms (derived from page data: ~54x, ~690x, ~2.6x); serialized size 25.3M vs 37.8M. Traverse alone is 67 ms for both. Compile time (clang-7 on Mac OS X): Cista++ `raw` 1.351 s vs cereal 1.827 s
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release from the README build steps (CMakeLists.txt adds no other optimization flags; C++20); compile-time table uses clang-7 on Mac OS X
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: The zero-copy 'offset' variant requires reading/writing in a fixed pointer-offset layout (no relocation), so both ends must share pointer width/endianness; the 'raw' variant (native pointers, relocatable) is far slower to serialize (3555ms) because of the extra relocation pass. Not schema-evolution-friendly like protobuf/capnproto without opt-in versioning.
caveats: Benchmark numbers come from felixguendling's own companion repo (cpp-serialization-benchmark), so they are first-party, but methodology (code, compiler, build type, CPU) is public, which is why it qualifies for tier A. The run is from 2021-12-18 (benchmark_result.txt) with Cista pinned as a submodule at d3492bf; the benchmark repo has not changed since 2021-12-31, and that run warns that CPU scaling was enabled. The 1.351 s compile time is for the `raw` variant, and `raw` serializes slower than cereal (650 ms vs 216 ms); the win is for the `offset` slim variant. The main cista README shows an older 2019 run (72 ms vs 239 ms serialize), which points the same direction. The very large deserialize speedup vs cereal is an architectural effect of zero-copy access (no parsing step), not a benchmarking artifact.

name: simdjson experimental_json_builder (C++26 reflection-based JSON serializer)
workload: Serializing native C++ structs to JSON using C++26 static reflection (P2996), measured on the twitter.json corpus and on an artificial/synthetic JSON dataset, reported in MB/s
claimed_speedup: Serialization throughput vs nlohmann/json, in MB/s. M3 Max: Twitter 1900 vs 100 (19x) and artificial 1800 vs 50 (36x). Intel Ice Lake: Twitter 1800 vs 110 (16x) and artificial 1400 vs 50 (28x). The page's summary is 'roughly 20x faster than nlohmann/json'. Two claims are qualitative only, with no numbers on the page: hand-written code 'can be slightly faster... (10% to 20%)', and 'We can be twice as fast as reflect-cpp'.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ from the Bloomberg experimental clang-p2996 fork (implements P2996 reflection; the page gives no version or commit). CMakeLists.txt hardcodes clang++ and defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG), with -freflection -stdlib=libc++ -std=c++26. This is the same at blog-date commit d3d2521 and at HEAD. Baseline: nlohmann/json 3.10.5 via CPM, and reflect-cpp v0.13.0 (patched).
hardware: Apple M3 Max MacBook Pro; an Intel Ice Lake machine (exact SKU not given)
tradeoffs: Requires an experimental, non-shipping C++26 compiler (Bloomberg's clang-p2996 fork with -freflection) rather than any release toolchain, so the technique is not usable in production yet. Same post reports it as ~2x faster than reflect-cpp (getml/reflect-cpp, an existing reflection-based serialization library) though exact reflect-cpp throughput numbers are not tabulated on the page. Hand-written (non-reflective) serialization code remains 10-20% faster than the generated code.
caveats: The repo README now opens with 'THIS REPOSITORY IS OBSOLETE. The functionality is part of the simdjson library'. The move has already happened: simdjson/simdjson, which is already catalogued, ships include/simdjson/generic/builder and benchmark/static_reflect. This standalone prototype is therefore the historical source of the numbers, not the place to get the code today. Since Dec 2024 the only commits are README edits, the last being the 2025-10-28 obsolete notice. The benchmark needs the experimental Bloomberg clang-p2996 fork (through Docker or a from-source Clang build), because the CMake setup hardcodes clang++ with -freflection and libc++. The baseline is the older nlohmann/json 3.10.5 (Jan 2022). The Ice Lake CPU is named only by microarchitecture, with no SKU. The comparisons with hand-written code and reflect-cpp have no published numbers.
found_via: Blog: Daniel Lemire, "Reflection-based JSON in C++ at Gigabytes per Second" (lemire.me, 2024-08-13), found via query "CppCon talk static reflection serialization code generation performance"; corroborated by the identically-titled CppCon 2025 talk (simdjson.github.io/simdjson_talks/cppcon2025) and the project's own README/CMakeLists on GitHub.

verification.tier_reason: Lemire's 2024-08-13 post has two MB/s tables comparing nlohmann/json with the C++26 serializer, and it names an Apple M3 Max and the Bloomberg clang-p2996 compiler. The benchmark code is public in the linked repo (benchmarks/src/benchmark_serialization_twitter.cpp and benchmark_serialization.cpp, with nlohmann/json 3.10.5 pinned in benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt). CMakeLists.txt at the blog-date commit d3d2521 forces a Release build (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG) with -freflection -stdlib=libc++ -std=c++26, so A holds for the M3 Max numbers. name: struct_pack (yalantinglibs)
workload: Serialize and deserialize vectors of 20 objects of three struct shapes (rect: 4 int32_t; person: int64_t id, std::string name, int age, double salary; nested Monster with strings, vectors and an enum), with pre-initialized objects and pre-allocated buffers, averaged over one million iterations; compared to protobuf, msgpack and flatbuffers (flatbuffers serialize only), using compile-time reflection (no macros for aggregate types)
claimed_speedup: (derived from page data, estimated from the PNG bar charts; each case is a vector of 20 objects) Serialize: struct_pack ~15-20 ns vs protobuf ~325 ns for 20 rect (~16-20x), ~100-110 ns vs ~540 ns for 20 person (~5x), ~665 ns vs ~2,900 ns for 20 monster (~4.4x); msgpack ~1,100-8,000 ns on the same cases. Deserialize: ~210 ns vs protobuf ~1,090 ns (20 rect, ~5x), ~960 ns vs ~2,130 ns (20 person, ~2.2x), ~7,600 ns vs ~17,500 ns (20 monster, ~2.3x). Repo README: '2-20x faster than protobuf'
compiler_and_flags: Alibaba Clang 13 (stated on the page). Flags are not on the page; cmake/build.cmake defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG), and the benchmark target defines STRUCT_PACK_OPTIMIZE and MSGPACK_NO_BOOST
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8163 CPU @ 2.50GHz
tradeoffs: Works best on aggregate structs; non-aggregate types (private members, custom order) need the YLT_REFL macro. Forward/backward compatibility requires explicitly wrapping new fields in struct_pack::compatible<T,version>. Ships as part of a large multi-library monorepo (yalantinglibs) rather than a standalone single-purpose dependency.
caveats: Numbers are only in PNG bar charts (no text table), so the figures are estimates from the chart axes. Each chart case is a vector of 20 objects. Alibaba Clang 13 is Alibaba's internal Clang build, which limits exact reproduction. The charts were added to the docs on 2023-07-05 and are not tied to a stated commit; the current benchmark.cpp also runs single-object cases and struct_pb. The docs compare against protobuf/msgpack/flatbuffers, not Boost.Serialization or cereal, hence baseline_in_list=false.

name: YAS (Yet Another Serialization)
workload: thekvs/cpp-serializers: serialize/deserialize a mixed object 1,000,000 times, averaged over 50 runs; fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark: serialize/deserialize a nested 'Monster' struct 300,000 times
claimed_speedup: thekvs suite: yas 302.7ms total vs boost 1195.04ms (~3.9x) and cereal 1052.46ms (~3.5x); fraillt suite (GCC 11): yas 2286ms ser/1770ms des vs boost 15126ms/12724ms (~6.6x/~7.2x) and cereal 10777ms/9088ms (~4.7x/~5.1x)
compiler_and_flags: thekvs suite: C++14, cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; the compiler for the published table is not stated (the README only says it was 'tested with Clang and GCC'). fraillt suite: GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1; CMakeLists.txt appends -O2 and defines NDEBUG with CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20 (the README/CI cmake call passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE).
hardware: thekvs: unspecified 'Intel Core i7' desktop, Ubuntu 16.04; fraillt: Ubuntu 20.04 x64, exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: No LICENSE file in the repository, so there is no explicit permission to reuse/modify the code despite it being publicly readable; project has had low commit activity in the last ~1.5 years.
caveats: The yas README says yas was created 'as a replacement of boost.serialization because of its insufficient speed' and cites both suites. Both suites are third-party with respect to yas: thekvs, and fraillt, who is the author of the competing library bitsery. Neither names an exact CPU model and thekvs does not name the compiler, so the evidence is not tier A. The win belongs to yas's default binary archive. In thekvs, 'yas-compact' (2063.34 ms) is slower than boost (1195.04) and cereal (1052.46). In fraillt, the std::stringstream-backed 'yas stream' case (GCC 10871/11182 ms) is no faster than cereal (10777/9088). Both runs are old: thekvs used yas 7.0.2 and boost 1.69 (repo last touched 2019); fraillt used yas 7.1.0, boost 1.77 and cereal 1.3.0. The repo has no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no license, but every sampled header under include/yas carries the Boost Software License 1.0 text.

name: bitsery
workload: Serialize/deserialize a vector of 50 randomly generated nested 'Monster' structs (fixed seed; vectors, strings, enums, weapons) 300,000 times after 5 warmup rounds, on Ubuntu 20.04 x64 with GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1 (fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark suite)
claimed_speedup: fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark README, 'general' test case. GCC 11: bitsery 1470 ms ser / 1524 ms des vs boost 15126/12724 ms (~10.3x/~8.3x) and cereal 10777/9088 ms (~7.3x/~6.0x). Clang 12.0.1: bitsery 2128/1832 ms vs boost 16011/13017 ms (~7.5x/~7.1x) and cereal 9977/8565 ms (~4.7x/~4.7x). Ratios derived from page data. bitsery's own README shows an older GCC 10.3.0 run: bitsery 1119/1166 ms vs boost 15391/12912 ms and cereal 10518/10245 ms.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1. CMakeLists.txt appends -O2, defines NDEBUG, MONSTERS=50 and SAMPLES=300000, and sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20. The README/CI cmake call passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE (the CI job names say 'Release').

tradeoffs: No implicit metadata/schema (compile-time only serialize() functions must be written per type); forward/backward compatibility and polymorphism require opting into specific extensions rather than being automatic like Boost.Serialization's archive system.
caveats: This is a first-party comparison: the benchmark repo belongs to bitsery's author (fraillt). The compiler and -O2 are stated but the CPU model is not, so the tier is C. The headline numbers in bitsery's README (1119/1166 ms, GCC 10.3.0) come from an older run than the GCC 11 / Clang 12 tables in the benchmark repo. bitsery's lead shrinks under Clang (~4.7x vs cereal). zpp_bits beats bitsery on the same page (GCC 733/693 ms). The page itself notes that the protobuf and flatbuffers comparisons are not fully fair because of conversion to the custom types.

name: Easy Reflection
baseline: nlohmann/json (JSON) and yaml-cpp (YAML); RapidJSON also measured
workload: Google Benchmark of serializing and deserializing one 2.9 KB user-profile document (benchmarks/data/boba_fett.json) to and from a reflected C++ struct, against nlohmann::json parse/dump, RapidJSON DOM parse/Writer and yaml-cpp load/emit of a generic node.
claimed_speedup: Per-operation times in microseconds read from the README chart (benchmarks/performance_chart.png, labelled Core i5): JSON serialization 2.8 vs nlohmann 9.3 (3.3x faster, derived from chart data); JSON deserialization 17.4 vs nlohmann 20.8 (1.2x), and 5.7 with the optional simdjson parser (3.6x); YAML serialization 3.4 vs yaml-cpp 331.8 (about 98x) and YAML deserialization 18.1 vs yaml-cpp 274.5 (about 15x), derived from chart data. RapidJSON on the same chart: 3.4 serialize, 7.4 parse. README text: 'JSON is faster than nlohmann json. Serialization is the same fast as rapid json, deserialization is a little faster with simdjson parser and more than twice slower without.'
hardware: Only 'Core i5' (image alt text); exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a clang-based code-generation step that parses [[er::reflect]] attributes and emits reflection code; C++17; native JSON, YAML 1.2 and a variable-length-integer binary format deserialize straight into typed objects (strings are converted to int, float and bool on load). Binary form is 61% of the JSON byte size (YAML 104%) per the repo's second chart, which is serialized size, not RAM.
caveats: Numbers exist only inside chart images (read from benchmarks/performance_chart.png); the README text gives no figures. Compiler, build type, flags and CPU model are not stated, and neither benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt nor the root CMakeLists.txt sets a build type or optimisation flags. The benchmark compares different jobs: Easy Reflection builds or dumps a typed struct, while nlohmann, RapidJSON and yaml-cpp build or dump a generic DOM. The README justifies this by saying the others do not convert strings to int, float or bool until accessed, which does not hold for nlohmann::json::parse or RapidJSON Document::Parse (both convert numbers and booleans at parse time). One small 2.9 KB document only (boba_fett.json, 2933 bytes). The yaml-cpp ratios (about 98x and 15x) are implausibly large for unstated flags; the yaml-cpp serialization case streams a YAML::Node through std::ostream, and the README itself says 'if I did the benchmark right'. Outputs are not checked for equivalence. The README calls the project 'mostly a proof of concept' and tells users who want this in production to use glaze instead. Repository archived and read-only since 2026-08-20 (the last commits that day only update the README; the last code change is 2025-02-04). [retier] Chart values only (serialization.cpp does real work) with compiler flags and CPU missing; typed-struct reflection vs generic DOM. The JSON writer never escapes strings and the native lexer leaves \n, \" and \uXXXX undecoded, so the 3.3x serialization gap skips the escape scan nlohmann and RapidJSON perform; the YAML writer emits every string unquoted, so the yaml-cpp rows are unequal work. Unknown keys throw std::runtime_error, doubles are written fixed with 9 decimals (lossy), round-trip tests use symbol-free strings only. The README claim that nlohmann and RapidJSON convert values lazily is wrong. Single 2.9 KB doc; proof of concept that points users to glaze. Archived 2026-08-20, last code change 2025-02-04.

Shortcomings: unstated flags and CPU, typed struct vs generic DOM, single 2.9 KB document, implausible yaml-cpp ratios, proof-of-concept project that points to glaze, archived.

retier.reason: Downgraded C to D: enricher found the JSON writer never escapes strings and the YAML writer emits all strings unquoted, so the measured serialization gaps (3.3x vs nlohmann/RapidJSON, 98x/15x vs yaml-cpp) skip work the baselines do and the output is wrong for strings that need escaping (uniwidth and fast_resize precedents; kept as directional since the chart values are real measurements of a flawed writer).

Compiler, build type, flags and CPU model are not stated and benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt sets no optimisation flags. The benchmark compares different jobs: Easy Reflection builds a typed struct, while nlohmann, RapidJSON and yaml-cpp build or dump a generic DOM (the README notes the others do not convert strings to int, float or bool until accessed). One small 2.9 KB document only. The yaml-cpp ratios (about 98x and 15x) are implausibly large; README itself says 'if I did the benchmark right'. The README calls the project 'mostly a proof of concept' and tells users who want this in production to use glaze instead. Repository archived and read-only since 2026-08-20.

name: Fast Binary Encoding (FBE)
workload: CppBenchmark fixtures (performance/*_serialize.cpp, *_deserialize.cpp): serialize/deserialize one Account with a wallet and three Orders (128-byte domain object; 120-280-byte messages depending on format), 5 attempts of 5 s each. The Protobuf path builds a fresh message and converts from the domain model on each operation.
claimed_speedup: CppSerialization README (CppBenchmark, Apple M1 Pro, run 2025-07-16): FBE 77 ns serialize / 84 ns deserialize vs Protobuf 322/351 ns (~4.2x/~4.2x, derived from page data). FBE is also faster than Cap'n Proto (247/184 ns) and than FlatBuffers at serialization (272 ns). FlatBuffers deserializes in 81 ns vs FBE's 84 ns, and SimpleBinaryEncoding (35/52 ns) and zpp::bits (34/37 ns) beat FBE on the same page.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated exactly; CppBenchmark report lists 'Process configuration: release' but no compiler name/version/flags
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (CppBenchmark reports 10 cores at 2.400 GHz), 32 GiB RAM, OS version 24.5.0 (Darwin), run 2025-07-16
tradeoffs: Requires its own IDL/schema and a code generator (similar to protobuf/Cap'n Proto), rather than serializing plain C++ structs directly; the linked benchmark uses a small, fixed message (~100-280 bytes), which may not reflect large-payload behavior.
caveats: This is first-party: FastBinaryEncoding and the comparison repo CppSerialization share the author (chronoxor). The CppBenchmark reports state the CPU (Apple M1 Pro) and 'release' but not the compiler or flags, so the tier is C. The table in FBE's own README (FBE 66/82 ns vs Protobuf 628/759 ns) is a stale 2018 run on an Intel Core i7-6700K / Windows 8 and does not match the current CppSerialization page. name: ser20
workload: Binary archive save to std::ostringstream and load from std::istringstream, 100-run averages, in sandbox/performance.cpp. That file is built by sandbox/CMakeLists.txt when Boost is found, not by doc/CMakeLists.txt. Data sets: vector<double> (1 to 1M), vector<uint8_t> (64M), vector<PoDStruct> (1 to 2M), vector<PoDChild> with a virtual base (1024, 32K), strings (200K to 20M chars), vector<string> (512 to 128K) and map<string,PoDStruct> (1024, 64K). name: chyaml
workload: Parses/materializes a 4.63MB synthetic YAML file (50,000 records, 15 alternating paired runs) plus an 8-shape workload matrix (mixed records, flat mapping, scalar sequence, nested mappings, flow sequences, quoted strings, sparse values/comments, long scalars) comparing chyaml's fast event tape against rapidyaml 0.16.0's arena tree.
claimed_speedup: chyaml's fast 8-byte event tape parses at about 391 MB/s vs 184 MB/s for rapidyaml 0.16.0 building its arena tree: about 2.13x faster with about 13.18x less incremental memory (6.18 MB vs 81.49 MB) on a 4,627,797-byte, 50,000-record input. Across the 8-shape matrix it is 1.16x-2.16x faster per shape (byte-weighted aggregate 1.92x, geometric mean 1.90x) and uses 1.63x-14.55x less memory. Event tape vs DOM tree is not a like-for-like comparison.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.44, CMake Release config with -DCHYAML_OPTIMIZE_FOR=SPEED (CMakeLists: /O2 /Gy /Gw /utf-8 on the chyaml target, IPO/LTCG on by default; executables /OPT:REF /OPT:ICF)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, Windows x64
tradeoffs: Reported speedups target chyaml's portable 8-byte fast-path event tape, which only covers common configuration-YAML shapes; input outside that subset falls back to a slower 'complete path' for full YAML 1.2.2 grammar (directives, complex keys, full block-scalar handling), where a separate matrix shows only 1.03x-7.22x; comparison executables link rapidyaml only for benchmarking, never into the shipped library.

The SIMD StructuralIter scan on 1 MiB is 4.2x (stable) / 9.2x (nightly-simd) faster than a memchr find_any_of loop.

name: yxml

It is not compared against pugixml or RapidXML; the only rivals are Expat, libxml2 and Mini-XML. The numbers are the author's own, from his project page, and nobody has reproduced them independently. The comparison is not like-for-like: libxml2 runs through the xmlTextReader pull API with most features configured out (--without-push/sax1/tree/valid...), and Expat runs with no callbacks. yxml is non-validating, with no DTD or custom-entity support, so it does less work. Each timing is a single `time` of the whole process, including loading a pre-cached file. At -Os yxml is slower than Expat on the Wiki file (1.67s vs 1.58s) and faster on Discogs (1.02s vs 1.20s), though it still beats libxml2 (3.01s/2.08s). claimed_speedup: vs libxml2 (README, Apple Silicon): SAX 2.5x (~1 KB) and 3.6x (~5 KB), DOM parse 1.4x (~5 KB), attribute lookup 1.9x, text extraction 2.6x, indexed child access 9% faster, XPath 1.3-4.0x on all 10 listed queries (several libxml2 cells are approximate, '~1 us'/'~3 us'). vs pugixml: attribute-set ~25x (measured against an approximate '~8-14 ms find+set' pugixml figure), serialize attr-heavy 2 MB 1.6x faster, but 1.3x slower on 10k-child append and 1.1x slower on text-heavy serialize.

name: quick-xml
workload: bemayer/xml-benchmark cross-language shootout (14 libraries, 7 languages). Each library runs in its own Docker container on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, and time is the mean of N auto-calibrated iterations. Each synthetic bucket (nominal 1KB-100MB) averages a wide/shallow file and a deep/narrow file. The deep files have 1,706-5,000 nesting levels and heavy indentation, so they are about 5.6 MiB (100KB label), 47.9 MiB (1MB and 10MB labels) and 100 MiB (100MB label). The 'other' bucket averages ~10MB DBLP and OpenStreetMap extracts. Operations: DOM parse, SAX/stream parse, XPath //*[@id], and serialize. quick-xml's DOM and SAX rows both run a Reader::read_event_into loop that builds no tree and does not touch attributes or unescape text. Its Serialize writes pre-parsed owned events with quick_xml::Writer.
claimed_speedup:
bemayer/xml-benchmark, run of 2026-09-01 (the page regenerates monthly). Throughput in MB/s; all ratios derived from page data.

Most representative is the real-world DBLP/OSM bucket ('other'):
- DOM Parse: quick-xml 715.3 vs pugixml 597.5 (1.2x) and libxml2 49.2 (14.5x)
- SAX/Stream: quick-xml 611.8 vs libxml2 331.8 (1.84x)
- Serialize: quick-xml 865.7 vs pugixml 707.6 (1.22x) and libxml2 499.1 (1.73x)

Synthetic buckets:
- DOM Parse 10MB: 3721.3 vs pugixml 1575.1 (2.4x) and libxml2 278.8 (13.3x)
- DOM Parse 100MB: 1619.1 vs 923.8 (1.75x) and 161.2 (10.0x)
- SAX/Stream 100MB: 1467.9 vs libxml2 822.0 (1.79x)
- Serialize 100MB: 1581.9 vs pugixml 1054.0 (1.5x) and libxml2 551.1 (2.87x)

quick-xml's 'DOM Parse' row does not build a tree. Its harness runs the same read_event_into loop as its SAX row, so the DOM ratios compare a pull tokenizer against full DOM builders.

quick-xml loses in three places. pugixml wins DOM Parse at 1KB (1977.9 vs 659.3; 0.001 vs 0.002 ms, at timer resolution). libxml2 shows higher Serialize throughput at 100KB (20100.9 vs 3748.3) and 1MB (15467.1 vs 2958.3), which is an artifact (see caveats). pugixml wins XPath Query, which quick-xml does not implement here.
compiler_and_flags: quick-xml: benchmarks/quick-xml/Cargo.toml sets [profile.release] opt-level = 3 and lto = true. The Dockerfile builds it with `cargo build --release` in the rust:slim image, so it uses the latest stable rustc at build time. The dependency is quick-xml = "*", so the crate version is whatever was newest and is not recorded. pugixml (master via CMake FetchContent) and both C++ harnesses are built with Debian bookworm g++ (12.2.0; the suite never prints it) via cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG), C++17. libxml2 itself is Debian bookworm's prebuilt package (2.9.14+dfsg), not compiled by the suite.
hardware: GitHub Actions 'ubuntu-latest' hosted runner (exact CPU model not stated; results refresh monthly via a cron CI job)
stars_or_usage: 1,570 GitHub stars; crates.io reports 431.8M total downloads, 117.1M recent downloads and 2,435 reverse dependencies (checked 2026-09-25)
tradeoffs: Written in Rust, so using it from C++ requires FFI/cxx bindings rather than direct linking; primarily an event-based (SAX-like) reader rather than a DOM-first API, though the same benchmark still measured a DOM-parse mode; does not implement XPath querying (pugixml wins that category in the same suite); much of libxml2's loss is tied to its heavier per-node allocation model (peak RSS 933.7 MB vs quick-xml's 106.1 MB at 100MB), so part of the win reflects allocation strategy, not only raw scanning speed.
caveats:
Evidence problems:
- The only C/C++ head-to-head is bemayer/xml-benchmark, a small third-party suite (1 star, no license, created 2026-04-06). It is one run a month on a shared CI runner with no CPU model, and the numbers drift between runs.
- quick-xml's 'DOM Parse' row is not a DOM parse. Its harness is the same streaming event loop as its SAX row, with lazy attribute parsing and no text unescaping. Comparing that row with pugixml or libxml2 building a full tree is apples to oranges. The fair comparisons are SAX/Stream against libxml2 SAX, and Serialize.
- The synthetic buckets are dominated by whitespace-heavy deep files, which inflates throughput for every library.

The libxml2 artifact:
- Debian's libxml2 2.9.14 halts at nesting depth 256 without XML_PARSE_HUGE (parser.c xmlParseElementStart calls xmlHaltParser). xmlParseMemory then returns NULL.
- As a result, libxml2's deep-file DOM and SAX timings measure a truncated parse, and its deep-file Serialize dumps a NULL document (a no-op).
- This favors libxml2, so quick-xml's wins over libxml2 are if anything understated. It also explains libxml2's 'wins' in Serialize at 100KB and 1MB.

Other limits:
- pugixml beats quick-xml at 1KB DOM parse (near timer resolution) and owns XPath.
- quick-xml is a Rust crate, so C++ users need FFI.

name: RapidXml
workload: DOM parse (bemayer/xml-benchmark: 14 libraries across 7 languages, 12 with DOM rows). Each bucket averages a synthetic wide/shallow file and a deep/narrow file. Because generate_data.py indents every level, the deep files are about 5.6 MiB (100KB label), 47.9 MiB (1MB and 10MB labels) and 100 MiB (100MB label), with 1,706 to 5,000 nesting levels. Only averages across the two shapes are published.
claimed_speedup: bemayer/xml-benchmark DOM Parse, run of 2026-09-01 (the page regenerates monthly). RapidXML vs libxml2 throughput: 1084.9 vs 278.8 MB/s in the 10MB bucket (26.93 vs 104.783 ms, ~3.9x, derived from page data); 638.2 vs 161.2 MB/s in the 100MB bucket (163.388 vs 646.685 ms, ~4.0x, derived from page data); 989.0 vs 79.1 MB/s in the 1KB bucket (~12.5x, derived from page data, but at 0.001 vs 0.013 ms, near timer resolution). libxml2 shows higher throughput in the 100KB bucket (3277.1 vs 2017.2 MB/s) and the 1MB bucket (2265.9 vs 1212.7 MB/s). The Dockerfile runs cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's default GCC Release flags are -O3 -DNDEBUG), and benchmarks/rapidxml/CMakeLists.txt adds CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 and -fpermissive. stars_or_usage: 2 stars on externpro/rapidxml, a CMake-packaged mirror. Upstream RapidXml's SourceForge page showed '3,065 This Week' downloads on 2026-09-25. bemayer/xml-benchmark uses the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip as its RapidXML entry. The verifier did not check the SpeedyXml-cpp mention.
tradeoffs: In-situ, destructive parser (mutates the source buffer); allocates DOM nodes from an internal per-instance pool, which becomes a scaling bottleneck at large file sizes versus newer arena/SoA designs (see libsimdxml and parshred entries, both of which cite this exact weakness); C++03-era single-header code with no active upstream maintainer since the 1.13 release (2009); canonical home is SourceForge (http://rapidxml.sourceforge.net/), this GitHub repo is a maintained third-party host of the original source
caveats: Only evidence is bemayer/xml-benchmark, a small third-party suite (1 star, no license, created 2026-04-06). It benchmarks the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip, not this repo, though the parser code is the same 1.13. Its size buckets are misleading: deep-shape files are 5.6-100 MiB with up to 5,000 nesting levels. libxml2 2.9.14 (Debian bookworm) stops at depth 256 without XML_PARSE_HUGE (parser.c nodePush calls xmlHaltParser). The libxml2 bench calls xmlParseMemory without checking the result, so its deep-file times measure a halted partial parse. This favors libxml2, so the ~3.9-4.0x RapidXml win at 10MB/100MB is if anything conservative. The 'libxml2 faster at 100KB/1MB' result is probably this artifact. Per-shape numbers are not published. The run is a single monthly run on a CI runner with no CPU model. RapidXml loses to pugixml at every size, so cite only libxml2 as the beaten baseline. RapidXml is a non-validating in-situ parser, while libxml2 builds a full DOM. The upstream parser has had no release since 1.13 (header dated 2009; SourceForge last updated 2013-04-26). externpro's recent commits (last 2026-08-31) are CMake/CI packaging only, so 'active' reflects packaging, not parser development.

name: VTD-XML
workload: bemayer/xml-benchmark cross-language shootout (14 libraries, 7 languages). Each library runs in its own Docker container on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner. Time is the mean of N auto-calibrated iterations (the page says 'median', but the harness divides total time by iterations). Each synthetic bucket (nominal 1KB-100MB) averages a wide/shallow file and a deep/narrow file. The deep files are about 5.6 MiB (100KB label), 47.9 MiB (1MB and 10MB labels) and 100 MiB (100MB label), with 1,706-5,000 nesting levels. VTD-XML's DOM Parse is VTDGen.setDoc(xml.clone()) + parse(false), which is namespace-unaware and builds no tree. It has no rows for deep files above 1KB.
claimed_speedup:
bemayer/xml-benchmark DOM Parse, run of 2026-09-01 (the page regenerates monthly). Mean times in ms, VTD-XML vs libxml2; all ratios derived from page data:
- 100KB: 0.542 vs 0.871 (1.6x)
- 1MB: 3.439 vs 10.788 (3.1x)
- 10MB: 21.45 vs 104.783 (4.9x)
- 100MB: 238.903 vs 646.685 (2.7x)
- 1KB: 0.036 vs 0.013 (VTD-XML is 2.8x slower)

These ratios are not like-for-like above 1KB. VTD-XML's rows at 100KB-100MB cover only the wide file. VTD-XML's MAX_DEPTH is 254, so it rejects the deep files (1,706-5,000 levels). Throughput x time on the page equals the wide-file size exactly. libxml2's rows average the wide file with a deep file that libxml2 2.9.14 halts at depth 256. Per-shape times are not published, so a same-file ratio cannot be derived.

VTD-XML's 'DOM Parse' builds a VTD token index, not a node tree. libxml2 builds and frees a full xmlDoc.

XPath //*[@id] runs on the same wide-only files for both libraries, and VTD-XML loses at every size:
- 1KB: 0.086 vs 0.005 ms (17x slower)
- 100KB: 0.907 vs 0.126 ms (7.2x slower)
- 1MB: 36.943 vs 2.509 ms (14.7x slower)
- 10MB: 392.963 vs 42.573 ms (9.2x slower)
- 100MB: 3837.515 vs 565.64 ms (6.8x slower)

The page's aggregate score ranks libxml2 (32.5) above VTD-XML (30.5).
compiler_and_flags: VTD-XML: com.ximpleware:vtd-xml resolved from the Maven range [2.0,), which gives 2.13.4 (Maven Central metadata lastUpdated 2017-08-10). The harness is built with maven:3-eclipse-temurin-21 and runs on eclipse-temurin:21-jre as a plain `java -jar` with no JVM flags. It does min(5, iterations) warm-up parses, and only 1 measured iteration on files over 50 MB. libxml2: Debian bookworm's prebuilt package (2.9.14). Its harness is built with bookworm g++ via cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG), C++17. The harness calls xmlParseMemory + xmlFreeDoc with no options (no XML_PARSE_HUGE).
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, with each library in its own Docker container (CPU model not published)
stars_or_usage: 35 stars and 11 forks on jzhang2004/vtd-xml, a full source copy of the SourceForge repo pushed by SourceForge project member jzhang2004 (last commit 2018-06-28). SourceForge: registered 2004-05-28, Last Update 2017-10-08, 74 downloads this week (checked 2026-09-25), latest file ximpleware-2.13-4-java.zip. Maven Central com.ximpleware:vtd-xml latest is 2.13.4.
tradeoffs: Requires a JVM; VTD's lazy/index-based model gives a fast DOM build but XPath queries afterward are then much slower than libxml2 (e.g. 3837.5ms vs 565.6ms at 100MB, derived from page data), so the win is DOM-parse-specific, not end-to-end; the project also ships native C/C++/C# ports per its site, but only the Java build was benchmarked here; dual GPLv2/commercial licensing, and the project homepage carries a notice terminating licenses for parties in litigation with XimpleWare.
caveats:
Evidence problems:
- The only head-to-head against libxml2 is bemayer/xml-benchmark, a small third-party suite (1 star, no license, created 2026-04-06). It runs once a month on a shared CI runner with no CPU model.
- Its DOM Parse buckets are not like-for-like. VTD-XML's MAX_DEPTH = 254 (VTDGen.java throws 'Depth exceeds MAX_DEPTH'), so VTD-XML fails on the 1,706-5,000-level deep files, and its 100KB-100MB rows cover only the wide file. libxml2's rows average the wide file with a deep file that libxml2 2.9.14 halts at depth 256. The displayed 1.6x-4.9x ratios therefore compare different file sets.
- VTD-XML's 'DOM Parse' builds a non-extractive token index, not a node tree.

Where VTD-XML loses:
- It is slower than libxml2 on XPath //*[@id] at every size (6.8x-17x).
- It loses DOM Parse at 1KB.
- pugixml beats it at 1KB, 10MB and 100MB.
- The page's aggregate score ranks libxml2 above VTD-XML.

Project limits:
- VTD-XML cannot parse documents deeper than 254 levels in standard mode.
- There has been no release since 2.13.4 (2017). The last GitHub commit is from 2018-06-28.
- The source headers are GPL-2.0-or-later but also cite US patents 7133857, 7260652 and 7761459. They add a clause that terminates the licenses of parties in litigation with XimpleWare, so check before copying.

name: Expat
baseline: libxml2 (DOM parse; Expat measured in SAX mode)
workload: Wall-clock parse (median of 3 repetitions) of a generated synthetic XML file (sample_1mb.xml and sample_10mb.xml; the 1 MB file has 16,824 elements, nesting up to 22, attributes, entities, CDATA, comments and processing instructions), Expat as SAX events versus libxml2 building a DOM tree.
claimed_speedup: 1 MB: Expat (SAX) 11.525 ms, 86.9 MB/s vs libxml2 (DOM) 26.507 ms, 37.8 MB/s (2.3x faster, derived from page data); 10 MB: 121.381 ms, 82.4 MB/s vs 263.196 ms, 38.0 MB/s (2.2x, derived); peak RSS 7.38 vs 24.81 MiB at 1 MB and 25.44 vs 197.37 MiB at 10 MB. Earlier run of the same file, 1 MB: Expat (SAX) 15.495 ms, 64.6 MB/s vs libxml2 (DOM) 35.168 ms, 28.5 MB/s (2.3x, derived).
hardware: Intel Core i7-4850HQ (Haswell, 2013 laptop). The cross-language table (expat 15.495 ms vs libxml2 35.168 ms) ran at the 2.3 GHz base clock with no turbo; the wall/CPU/memory table (11.525 vs 26.507 ms, 121.381 vs 263.196 ms) is the 24.09.2026 run ab_quick_20260924_001320 at about 3.3 GHz (schedutil governor, turbo on, scaling_max_freq 3.5 GHz, load about 2.0 at start).
tradeoffs: Non-validating, stream-oriented push parser in C with no tree, so memory stays near input size (7.38 MiB peak at 1 MB in the table above) but the caller must build any document structure; libxml2 additionally offers DOM, validation, XPath and HTML parsing.
caveats: Weak and contested evidence. Expat's own README says only 'Fast streaming XML parser written in C99 with >90% test coverage', with no numbers. The figures come from the README of a competing 2026 project (KrzysztofKowalski/libsimdxml, 0 stars, 18 commits, a C++23 port of the Rust simdxml) that lists expat and libxml2 only as references. The harness is not public: the README's tmp/benchmark/orchestrator.sh and tools/rss_sampler.py are not in the repository. Expat and libxml2 versions, compiler and flags are not stated. The two libsimdxml tables were taken at different clocks (2.3 GHz base without turbo for the 15.495/35.168 ms cross-language table; about 3.3 GHz with turbo for the 11.525/26.507 and 121.381/263.196 ms wall/CPU/memory table), so ratios hold only within a table. The compared modes differ (Expat streaming SAX events vs libxml2 building a full DOM tree, which also explains the 25.44 vs 197.37 MiB peak RSS at 10 MB), so this is not like-for-like; the win belongs to streaming, not to the parser. Like-for-like data points the other way: bemayer/xml-benchmark (report/index.html committed, run dated 2026-04-06T17:17:26Z, runner 'local', hardware, compiler and versions not stated, Docker images with latest versions) has libxml2 SAX/Stream faster than Expat at every size: 1KB 0.028 vs 0.046 ms, 100KB 2.104 vs 10.178 ms, 1MB 39.606 vs 70.714 ms, 10MB 110.529 vs 145.468 ms, 100MB 592.34 vs 933.022 ms, and 104.826 vs 234.468 ms in a group labelled 'other' (that report's time and throughput columns imply input sizes other than the group labels, e.g. the '1MB' group works out to about 24 MB, so its labels are unreliable, but each within-group comparison favours libxml2). Search snippets of older posts (pages not opened, snippet only) disagree: a 2011 OSM-dev post has Expat about 10% faster than libxml2 on OSM data, a 2006 GNOME xml-list post has libxml2 about 30% faster on most test data, and an OpenOffice wiki page calls libxml2 SAX the fastest. Security: the libexpat repo shows a caution banner 'Expat has unfixed security issues' pointing to issue #1160 (open since 2026-03-06), which tracks about 30 non-public reports (DoS loops, NULL function-pointer dereferences, out-of-bounds access, UTF-16 surrogate validation).

name: frxml
workload: Parses randomly generated XML documents: pugixml-built trees of 50-1000 nodes with random 5-char element names and one attribute each, max depth 300, about 0-330 KiB. Timed with google/benchmark at 3 iterations per size against pugixml, RapidXML, tinyxml2 and libxml2 (DOM parse). Legacy Oct-2024 harness test/src/main.cxx at commit 06b3b12; allocated bytes counted by wrapping malloc.
claimed_speedup: Chart plots parse time relative to frxml (lower = faster), values read from log-scale Figure_1.png: libxml2 is ~1.8-9x slower than frxml (largest at the smallest inputs) and tinyxml2 ~2.6-5x slower. pugixml (~0.8-0.9x, dipping to ~0.4x at ~260-290 KiB) and RapidXML (~0.8-0.95x, ~0.4x at ~260-290 KiB) are FASTER than frxml at nearly all sizes. Memory: frxml allocates less than pugixml, tinyxml2 and libxml2 throughout, but RapidXML allocates less than frxml below ~45 KiB.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler unstated; frxml library built with -O3 -march=native (frxml/CMakeLists.txt at commit 06b3b12); pugixml, tinyxml2 and libxml2 come from system packages via find_package, flags unknown
tradeoffs: Zero-copy/single-pass design explicitly omits entity and DOCTYPE/ENTITY decoding to stay zero-copy, and only supports a limited XML 1.0 subset; goal of O(n) memory regardless of nesting depth.
caveats: The chart shows frxml SLOWER than pugixml and RapidXML, the fast incumbents in this category; it only beats libxml2 and tinyxml2. The numbers exist only as a chart image (Figure_1.png, Oct 2024) from the legacy implementation. The code was rewritten in Aug-Sep 2025 with a new harness (frxml-test/lib/main.cxx, vs pugixml/tinyxml2 on UW XML datasets) that has no published results, yet README still shows the old figure. No compiler or CPU stated; only 3 iterations per size. Limited XML 1.0 support: no DOCTYPE/ENTITY, no entity decoding. The repository is archived.

name: libsimdxml
workload: Single-threaded parse of the project's own deterministic synthetic XML (16,824 elements at 1 MB, depth up to 22, attributes, entities, CDATA, comments, PIs) into libsimdxml's structural index. Measured in MB/s and peak RSS against pugixml 1.16 (in-situ DOM), libxml2 DOM, expat SAX and parsers in other languages. Speed numbers are published only for 1/5/10 MB (the 24.09 run covers only 1 and 10 MB). The 15-30 MB corpora are listed but have no published numbers.
claimed_speedup: Base-clock run 165913 (15.09.2026, i7-4850HQ at 2.3 GHz, no turbo): 245.7 vs 206.3 MB/s (1 MB), 261.4 vs 227.8 (5 MB) and 285.2 vs 229.2 (10 MB) against pugixml 1.16 in-situ. The README states this as 1.19x/1.15x/1.24x. In the same run libxml2 DOM reached 28.5 MB/s at 1 MB (~8.6x, derived from page data). A later turbo-on C++-only run (24.09.2026) gives 283.0 vs 271.1 MB/s (1 MB) and 296.5 vs 278.5 (10 MB) against pugixml (~1.04x/~1.06x, derived from page data). Against libxml2 DOM that run gives 37.8 and 38.0 MB/s (~7.5x/~7.8x, derived from page data). The README notes that at 10 MB libsimdxml uses ~8% more CPU than pugixml. The README also states 1.26x/1.35x/1.47x over Rust quick-xml 0.36 at 1/5/10 MB.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4850HQ (Haswell, 2013 laptop), fixed at 2.3GHz base clock with turbo off for the headline speed table (a separate reference table notes a ~3.3GHz turbo-on run, explicitly not to be mixed with the base-clock numbers)

tradeoffs: Runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX2/SSE4.2/NEON/scalar all compiled into one binary, selected via [[gnu::target]]); structure-of-arrays index instead of per-node heap allocation; does not target HTML; excludes tinyxml2 and fast-xml-parser from its cross-language table because they error out on the benchmark's processing-instruction corpus

The README gives the pugixml lead as 1.15-1.24x at base clock, but the later turbo-on run shows only ~4-6% wall-time lead and ~8% more CPU at 10 MB. It is a C++ port of the Rust simdxml crate. 0 stars, repo created 2026-09-07, with no third-party review.

name: rusty_xml (Remade-With-Rust)
workload: CLI-vs-CLI parse without output (xmllint --noout against rxmlint --noout, --repeat inner loop) on big-attr.xml (627KB), big-1m.xml (1.27MB), big-300k.xml (309KB) and slashdot.xml (3.7KB x 10000). The run is single core, CPU-time metric, ABBA-interleaved, with N=20 pairs and a C-vs-C null arm per row.
claimed_speedup: As shipped (rxmlint linked with rusty_alloc against xmllint on the system allocator), CLI parse-noout: 1.55x-2.31x faster (derived from page data). The us/C ratios are 0.447x on big-attr.xml (83.25 vs 37.18 MB/s), 0.644x on big-1m.xml (115.74 vs 74.56), 0.625x on big-300k.xml (125.56 vs 78.47) and 0.432x on slashdot.xml (118.05 vs 50.98). All four files show 20/20 paired wins at z=+4.47. The README headline is '1.6x to 2.2x faster'. With the same allocator on both sides (the parser alone, N=11), the page reports big-attr 0.80x (~1.25x faster, derived) and big-300k 1.07x (rusty_xml ~7% slower). The author states that roughly half the margin is the allocator.
compiler_and_flags: rxmlint built with `cargo build -p rusty_xml-cli --release` (rustc version not stated) and linked with rusty_alloc. libxml2 is a pinned prebuilt v2.15.3 xmllint.exe on the system allocator. Parse options differ: C defaults to XML_PARSE_COMPACT | XML_PARSE_BIG_LINES, and rxmlint forces NONET | NO_XXE.
hardware: CPU model not stated. The harness is Windows PowerShell (xmllint.exe/rxmlint.exe), pinned to core 4 at High priority, and measures CPU time.
tradeoffs: Author states roughly half the speed advantage comes from rusty_alloc (pure-Rust mimalloc) vs libxml2's system allocator, not the parsing algorithm itself; ground-up reimplementation of libxml2's algorithms (not a binding), so feature completeness (full XPath, validation) is still catching up
caveats: The headline ratio is 'as shipped' and includes rusty_alloc (a pure-Rust mimalloc port) against libxml2 on the system allocator. With the same allocator, the author measures only 0.80x on big-attr and 1.07x on big-300k, where rusty_xml is slower, and says quoting the as-shipped ratio as a parser result would be wrong. The slashdot.xml row is flattered because xmllint re-opens and re-reads the file on every --repeat. This is CLI-vs-CLI with different parse flags, not a kernel A/B. The repo is very new (created 2026-08-27, 1 star). The CPU model, OS details and rustc version are not stated. The numbers are the author's own and are not independently reproduced.
